item.title: [El Nacional — La voz de todos] ¡En observación! Los Yankees esperan 48 horas para conocer el alcance de la molestia de Aaron Judge
item.source: El Nacional — La voz de todos
item.dc:creator: Agencia EFE
item.description: MLB | ¡En observación! Los Yankees esperan 48 horas para conocer el alcance de la molestia de Aaron Judge "No vamos a especular de una forma u otra. Simplemente veremos cómo responde", indicó el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. Redacción Deportes — El cuerpo médico de los Yankees de Nueva York esperará un periodo de 48 horas para realizar las pruebas correspondientes y determinar la gravedad de la molestia muscular de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro de este miércoles a poc
item.content:encoded:
MLB |
¡En observación! Los Yankees esperan 48 horas para conocer el alcance de la molestia de Aaron Judge
"No vamos a especular de una forma u otra. Simplemente veremos cómo responde", indicó el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone.
Redacción Deportes — El cuerpo médico de los Yankees de Nueva York esperará un periodo de 48 horas para realizar las pruebas correspondientes y determinar la gravedad de la molestia muscular de Aaron Judge, quien tuvo que abandonar el encuentro de este miércoles a pocos días de haber superado su última estancia en la lista de lesionados.
"No vamos a especular de una forma u otra. Simplemente veremos cómo responde", indicó el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone.
Judge fue retirado en la sexta entrada del encuentro que los Yankees perdieron por 5-4 en 13 episodios, después de comenzar a sentir rigidez en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha desde el primer episodio.
El equipo tiene programado un día libre este jueves, lo que permitirá a Judge recibir tratamiento y observar la respuesta de la zona afectada antes de tomar una decisión sobre su disponibilidad para los próximos partidos.
Judge, que regresó a la alineación el pasado 8 de septiembre después de permanecer cerca de tres meses fuera, explicó que no pudo identificar un movimiento específico que desencadenó la molestia y confió en que se trate de un problema menor.
También te puede interesar:
"Siento que lidias con esto en cada Spring Training. Ya sabes, por lo general, al inicio de la temporada una vez que empiezas a aumentar la intensidad, surgen cosas, y ahí es donde hemos estado", comentó Judge.
"Afortunadamente, en todo este tiempo desde que regresé, nada nos ha molestado. Así que espero que sea solo algo pequeño y estemos de vuelta pronto", añadió.
El capitán de los Yankees decidió salir del encuentro después de intentar continuar pese a la molestia, consciente de la importancia de preservar su estado físico en el tramo decisivo de la temporada.
"Traté de disimularlo y ver hasta dónde podíamos llegar, porque estos juegos son importantes en la recta final", expresó Judge. "Pero después de hablarlo un poco, pensé que lo correcto era salir, para no costarle al equipo en el terreno o en las bases".
La salida se produjo después de que Judge disputara seis encuentros consecutivos desde su regreso, por lo que el martes había tenido un día de descanso programado.
El jugador había comenzado a recuperar ritmo ofensivo y el lunes conectó su primer cuadrangular desde su regreso, antes de marcharse del partido del miércoles tras poncharse en sus dos primeros turnos frente al abridor de los Mellizos, Zebby Matthews.
"No anticipaba someterse a exámenes médicos", señaló Judge tras el encuentro, aunque los Yankees mantendrán bajo observación la molestia durante el día libre.
"Obviamente es una figura clave en lo que hacemos", comentó Boone. "Con suerte lo trataremos, nos desharemos de eso y será un factor en algún momento".
Los Yankees afrontan las últimas semanas de la temporada con Judge como una de sus principales piezas ofensivas y deberán esperar su recuperación antes de definir si estará disponible para las próximas series.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are officially IN the MLB playoff picture, as they recently clinched a postseason berth.
While the Yankees still have a small percentage chance to win the AL East, they will likely be in the AL Wild Card round, playing the Boston Red Sox.
In such a big series, decisions will have to be made regarding who gets a 26-man roster spot.
One player who is on the outside looking in and will likely be left off is Luis Gil.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Get Strong Jasson Dominguez Message Ahead of MLB Playoffs
Yankees Urged to Leave Luis Gil Off Playoff Roster
Recently, FanSided.com writer Jake Elman predicted a handful of players who will be 'dumped' from the playoff roster, or essentially dumped from the 26-man fold.
"But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don't expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt's return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn't shown that he's worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he'd be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates. "
Gil has pitched just 23.1 innings for the Yankees this season, and carries a 5.40 ERA in that span.
So, yeah, it's fair to assume his spot on the playoff roster may not be safe.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
What Has Luis Gil Done in His MLB Career
Luis Gil has technically pitched in five seasons with the New York Yankees.
He briefly pitched in 2021 and 2022 with the club, but did not pitch at all in MLB in 2023 before bursting onto the scene in 2024 (AL Rookie of the Year).
However, since earning that top accolade, he has not been consistent as a member in the Yankees rotation.
Across 265.1 total IP in his career, Gil holds a very respectable 3.66 ERA, but perhaps his absence from the Bigs is a product of the Yankees' loaded rotation, rather than his individual ability.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Reveal Edwin Diaz Plans Amid Looming Return

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: The New York Yankees, much like all the other postseason teams in MLB, will have to make tough decisions when it comes to their October roster. It's a 26-man roster in October across MLB, and no team can carry more than 13 pitchers. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees, much like all the other postseason teams in MLB, will have to make tough decisions when it comes to their October roster.
It's a 26-man roster in October across MLB, and no team can carry more than 13 pitchers. How a club opts to round out its roster is entirely up to them, but speaking to the New York Yankees, a recent postseason projection leaves players like Paul Goldschmidt on the fringe.
So, what should the Yankees do with their playoff roster, and who needs to be left off?
More MLB on Heavy: MLB World Reacts to George Lombard Jr. Blunder in Yankees-Twins Game
Yankees Urged to Dump Paul Goldschmidt from Playoff Roster
In a recent piece for FanSided.com, writer Jake Elman predicts a handful of Yankees players who could be dumped from the postseason roster, and Goldschmidt's name pops up:
"Let's get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he's only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed. The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt's favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that's not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you'd finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job."
Paul Goldschmidt has been somewhat of a solid contributor for the Yankees this season, playing in 101 games and clubbing 18 home runs and 12 doubles, so his playoff status is certainly up for debate at this moment.
After all, not every team has a lefty masher like Goldy who would certainly be used purely as a platoon.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 2 Roster Moves Before Reds Game
Should Paul Goldschmidt Make the Yankees Playoff Roster?
It's obviously all speculation on behalf of Elman, but he does bring up a big crossroads the Yankees will be at when it comes to a Goldschmidt decision.
The 39-year-old Goldy is also batting .253 this season with an OPS+ of 113, so he's an above-average hitter by 13% in MLB, against both righties and lefties.
Good thing I am not in the position to be making decisions like this, but Yankees fans, comment below what you would do with Paul Goldschmidt this October? And would he be part of your ideal Yankees batting order?
More MLB on Heavy: Chicago Cubs Announce Ian Happ News After Bad Braves Loss

item.title: [MLB.com] Will Yankees' postseason first-timers prove to be ready for the moment?
item.dc:creator: Patrick Donnelly
item.description: It’s common to think of the Yankees as a playoff-tested team. After all, this is the eighth time in nine years that they’ve made the postseason under manager Aaron Boone. And a quick look at some of their regulars shows a lineup that varies between a little bit and a wealth of October experience. Player No. of Career Playoff Games Cody Bellinger 76 Aaron Judge 65 Paul Goldschmidt 29 Trent Grisham 26 Jazz Chisholm, Jr.
item.content:encoded:
It’s common to think of the Yankees as a playoff-tested team. After all, this is the eighth time in nine years that they’ve made the postseason under manager Aaron Boone. And a quick look at some of their regulars shows a lineup that varies between a little bit and a wealth of October experience.
Player No. of Career Playoff Games
Cody Bellinger                     76
Aaron Judge                        65
Paul Goldschmidt                29
Trent Grisham                      26
Jazz Chisholm, Jr.                 24
Austin Wells                          21
Anthony Volpe                     21
Amed Rosario                      11
Ryan McMahon                   10
Ben Rice                               6
José Caballero                     3
But a few names are missing from that list: Shortstop George Lombard Jr., outfielder Spencer Jones, first baseman Luis García Jr. and outfielder Heliot Ramos. Those four have never played in the postseason, either with the Yankees or -- as is the case with García and Ramos -- with their previous teams.
Now, it’s possible that some of the injured veteran players -- Grisham and Chisholm, specifically -- could return to the lineup and send some of those new faces to the bench or off the playoff roster entirely. But it’s safe to say the Yankees are going to be counting on at least a few playoff newbies next month in their quest to win their first World Series since 2009.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said his youngsters and playoff newcomers have another advantage over players who are coming of age in other markets.
“You play for the Yankees, you play in New York,” he said, “it has a way of getting you ready for the postseason.”
This has been something of a transitional year in the Major Leagues. Check out the first round of the 2023 Draft if you want proof. No fewer than 19 of the 37 first-round and sandwich picks have debuted, and many of them are already impact players with their teams.
“Players are getting to the big leagues at a very quick pace now and at a young age,” said Tigers manager A.J. Hinch, who has welcomed No. 3 pick Max Clark and AL Rookie of the Year favorite Kevin McGonigle to Detroit this year. “I don't think they're as wowed by the big steps that they're taking.”
For the Yankees, that class includes Lombard, who has acclimated nicely since being called up in early August. And Jones was recently lauded by none other than Aaron Judge, who said the rookie outfielder has “really evolved every single time he got called up, gotten a little bit better and a little bit better.”
Of course, there will be hiccups along the way. On Wednesday, Jones went 0-for-6 with five strikeouts and committed an error when he dropped a fly ball in center field. And Lombard couldn’t come up with a Victor Caratini grounder in the 13th that was ruled a single as the Twins walked off the Yankees.
But anyone who follows baseball knows bad days and bad plays are all part of the growth cycle of a Major League player. The key is to learn from them so you can limit them going forward. And all of it -- the good, the bad and the occasionally ugly -- helps prepare a young player for his first time playing in the crucible of October baseball.
The world is about to find out just how ready the young Yankees are. But Jones offered a bit of reassurance on Monday as he soaked up the post-clinch locker room celebration at Target Field.
“I think for us, we play better when the crowd gets louder,” he said. “I’m really excited for what’s to come.”

item.content:encoded:
Keith Law is one of the most widely respected prospects writers in baseball, and one thing he tries to do is explain why he gets certain players wrong.
In a new article on Thursday, he dove into New York Yankees star Ben Rice, whom he never viewed as a high-ranking prospect.
Of course, Law was not alone in his assessment.
Rice went to Dartmouth, not known as a baseball powerhouse, and he was a 12th-round pick in the 2021 MLB Draft, having missed out on a lot of college baseball because of the COVID-19 pandemic and ending up with just one homer in his college career.
Nothing about Rice’s outward pedigree screamed future star.
But through Sept. 16, Rice has belted 38 home runs and driven in 92 runs in the 2026 MLB season. Clearly, he’s a star.
The 27-year old lefty slugger just wasn’t always seen this way.
What Prospect Rankings Got Wrong
One of the first things that struck Law was that Rice was a catcher who wasn’t going to stay a catcher. That’s always a negative.
Rice also didn’t have an early start in the minor leagues, and so he was always older than most at his level.
“Even when he started producing in the minor leagues, with a 20-homer season across three levels in 2023, he was old for the levels he played at and didn’t have a position — he was a catcher with no shot to stay there,” Law wrote on Thursday. “His swing was extremely uphill, prioritizing power over everything else, and in his first stint in the majors in 2024, pitchers exploited that swing path, leading to his first struggles in pro ball.”
It turns out that Rice kept making the changes and improvements that would help him become a quality big leaguer, though.
“Rice went out that offseason and worked on his swing and his body, gaining enough strength to improve his bat speed and, naturally, his contact quality,” Law writes. “It wasn’t his first rodeo — he’d changed his stance and swing while in college — but this change was more dramatic, with a much more open setup and a stride that didn’t close himself off, helping him roll over to the right side less often and, at least in 2025, pull the ball in the air more. The change also made him less vulnerable on stuff middle-in; in 2024, he whiffed on 25 percent of pitches on the inner third, then cut that to 11.3 percent in 2025 and 11.9 percent so far this year. He’s still not a catcher, but he’s a top-10 bat in the majors this year.”
Keith Law on Cam Schlittler
Law goes on in the same blurb to note that he also never saw Yankees pitching star Cam Schlittler turning out to be this good.
“He barely threw a sinker at all when I saw him, and used it just 6.1 percent of the time in the majors last year, but this year he’s used it 19.6 percent of the time,” Law writes. “Schlittler has thrown something other than one of his three fastballs just 10.6 percent of the time this year. Only Chad Patrick throws fewer non-fastballs among starters with 100+ innings this year; Misiorowski is fourth on the list at 18.3 percent.”
A prospect analyst would want to see more than just a good fastball to be high on a pitcher.
Schlittler’s fastball variety pack has turned out to be so good that he’s hardly needed anything else, a total outlier but a total star.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Ex-player on Aaron Judge not taking rehab assignment appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees recently got a scare when superstar Aaron Judge exited their game against the Minnesota Twins with leg tightness. The incident came just days after Judge had made his highly anticipated return to the lineup after a ribcage injury that kept him out of the lineup for months, and the Yankees ended up losing the game 5-4.
Now, former player AJ Pierzynski has weighed in on how Judge's decision not to go on a rehab assignment before returning from the original injury may have played a role in this latest scare.
"This is why you go on a rehab assignment, especially when you missed as long as Aaron Judge did. He said it, this is like spring training, so you try to get the soreness and other little things that pop up out of the way by going on a rehab assignment," he said, per Foul Territory on X, formerly Twitter. "He didn't do that, he didn't want to do that."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Indeed, Judge passed up the opportunity to go on a rehab assignment prior to making his return to the big leagues. Of course, it's impossible to know whether things would have played out differently with this recent injury scare had he opted to take such an assignment, but clearly, Pierzynski believes it couldn't have hurt.
Thankfully, Judge's leg injury doesn't appear to be anything too severe, and the star is hoping to ramp up even more before the playoffs begin in just a couple of weeks, with New York hoping to turn in a better performance than last year's ALDS loss.
New York will next take the field on Friday evening vs the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Related: Yankees rookie Spencer Jones joins Aaron Judge club nobody wants in loss to Twins
Related: Yankees' Aaron Judge shares his side of story about leg tightness concern

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Why Anthony Volpe Deserves Postseason Roster Spot Over Amed Rosario
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have a lot of decisions to make for their postseason roster, from lineup construction to the outfield, rotation, and bullpen, to managing guys coming back from injury. Outside of the team's core foundation, almost nothing is settled, especially on the bubble.
One of those bubble spots entails the backup infielders behind a hopefully healthy Jazz Chisholm Jr., George Lombard Jr., and Ryan McMahon. As of right now, the Yankees have three of them on the roster: José Caballero, Amed Rosario, and Anthony Volpe. The former has a secured spot due to his speed and versatility, but the latter two aren't as secure.
It's entirely possible the Yankees carry 14 position players on the playoff roster, but that means somebody will have to go for Chisholm when he returns. It's widely believed the corresponding move will be to send Volpe back to the minors, but what if the Yankees went another direction?
Here's why Volpe should be the one who lands that final infield spot instead of Rosario, and how the Yankees can handle the roster math:
New look Anthony Volpe can provide value to Yankees
I am personally not drinking the Kool-Aid of any tangible offensive improvements for Volpe, at least in the short term. What he did at Triple-A was feast on inferior pitchers with his opposite-field approach, something that doesn't have a 1-to-1 conversion rate in the big leagues. That said, we know what he is throughout his career: a mediocre hitter with a career 84 OPS+ and an 89 OPS+ this season in 62 games entering Wednesday.
That said, the ability to hit is maybe the least important aspect for a bench player, particularly one on a team that will have pinch-hitting options on both sides of the plate but needs defenders to replace them.
Volpe was not a fit for this roster when he only played shortstop, something that he would no longer get a chance to do with Lombard entrenched at the position. Upon his demotion to Triple-A, he got experience at second and third base, with the former being the position he's played almost every day since he was recalled after Chisholm's injury. Early returns are positive there.
At this point, we can directly compare Volpe to Rosario, who has also predominantly played second and third base when he has played. While offense is likely not on the 25-year-old's side, defense and baserunning certainly are. He's a vastly superior defender, posting a 3 DRS, 5 FRV, and 5 OAA at shortstop earlier this season.
Volpe is also a much more aggressive baserunner, recording 10 stolen bases and being one of baseball's best at stealing third base, an extremely critical skill to have in close playoff games.
And all of this assumes that Volpe's bat remains as bad as it's been throughout his career. But what if he did make positive adjustments? What if this new approach, coupled with his improved plate discipline from Opening Day, makes him playable, even as a platoon bat? He's already had a few clutch hits, as we saw in the Twins' series.
Amed Rosario's 2026 struggles make him expendable
The one thing that Rosario has on Volpe is his hitting ability, particularly against left-handed pitching, but we've gotten enough samples this season to determine whether a player's reputation actually backs up the results. For Rosario? It's not pretty.
A career .287 hitter against lefties, Rosario is down to just .200 with a .602 OPS against them in 151 plate appearances, something that goes beyond a small sample size. His strikeout rate against them at 21.1 percent is the highest it's been in a decade, while his quality of contact has similarly tanked, even if he's been very unlucky (.262 wOBA vs. .306 xwOBA). Compare this to Volpe, who's slashing a mediocre (but better) .253/.323/.373 against lefties this season, so is Rosario's best strength now a weakness?
He's had pretty hefty reverse splits this season, which completely goes against why he was signed. The Yankees have significantly better options on both sides of the ball against righties, so it doesn't help them at all. When you factor in his defensive shortcomings? He really seems like someone who should be on the chopping block.
Rosario is a guy who can play corner outfield and three infield positions, but plays none of them well. In just 303 innings this season at third base, he has -8 OAA and -7 FRV. He's also managed to be minor negatives in just 48 combined innings in left field, right field, and second base. On a rate basis, he's arguably the worst defender in baseball, something that would be muted if his bat was going (or if the DH spot was more accessible).
He's not a bad baserunner at all. In fact, he's one of the faster guys on the team in terms of sprint speed, but the few times he's on base this season, he's rarely in motion. He has just three stolen bases in the last two seasons and has been a net-negative baserunner according to Baseball Savant's Baserunning Runs metric due to a lack of aggressiveness in taking the extra base.
When your one strength isn't much of a strength anymore, and your usage on the roster is diminished, it has us asking how Volpe could help the team with its roster construction in the postseason.
How the roster shakes out
It wouldn't even be a major roster disruptor. Rosario is almost always the last guy on the bench because of how little the team trusts him defensively. If his bat was that much of an upgrade in a platoon situation, they'd make that trade, but it hasn't.
Come playoff time, I can see a world where the Yankees play Volpe at second or third base in place of McMahon or Chisholm against a left-handed pitcher to increase the at-bat quality without a massive defensive drop-off. It would also give them another pinch-running option they might need in late and close situations, as one of the best base stealers on the team.
I don't expect the Yankees to want to get rid of Rosario, though. He can be left off the playoff roster without a problem. But he can't be removed before then, which could cause an issue if Chisholm is likely to return before the postseason begins.
Therefore, a potential solution could be to send a pitcher down and play with an extra position player down the stretch, but the team is running out of players with options. Volpe could also go down just to fit puzzle pieces and return a few days later.
Ultimately, whatever the Yankees decide, it might not be the difference between a playoff series or even a playoff game, but margins are margins. This has not been a team that has won enough close games late, so giving yourself as much of an advantage in those situations is paramount.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will have a decision to make when Jazz Chisholm Jr. is back from the injured list.
Anthony Volpe is up in Chisholm's place, but he is looking like a completely different hitter after a stint in Triple-A. He has made some changes and is hitting .348/.400/.565 with a home run, two doubles, four stolen bases and seven RBIs. Before he was optioned, he had a .240 batting average and a .646 OPS with one home run in 56 games.
When Chisholm is back, he will go back to starting every day. Even though it's a down year for him, he had really turned things around before his injury. Before his injury, Chisholm was slashing .313/.398/.835 and had 10 stolen bases since Aug. 9.
If Volpe stays hot, the Yankees cannot really afford to keep him out of the lineup. On the other hand, they cannot bench Chisholm, who was swinging it well and has been a starter all year. What can they do then? Well, the Brewers could leave Volpe at second base and play Chisholm at third base.
Ryan McMahon has not been great at third base, and if Chisholm is swinging the bat like he was for a month before his injury, he would easily be the best option there. He is not as strong a defender there, but the Yankees would be much better offensively without McMahon in the lineup.
Of course, this is dependent on Volpe staying hot and Chisholm picking up where he left off. If both of those don't happen, it becomes a situation where the Yankees need to pick one or the other, and it seems like Chisholm would get the nod.
More MLB: Dave Roberts' Shohei Ohtani Update Is Not Exactly Inspiring

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are headed to the MLB playoffs! But they have a lot to figure out before they *likely* have to face the Boston Red Sox in a 3-game Wild Card series.
A big storyline surrounding the Yankees right now is what manager Aaron Boone will do with Anthony Volpe when Jazz Chisholm Jr. returns.
Since Jazz went to the IL (and Volpe was called up). Volpe has had his fair share of moments, and it begs the question: What will the Yankees’ infield layout look like?
Yankees fans may hate to admit it, but with Volpe’s previous playoff experience, it might be wise to give the kid a shot in October.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Predicted to ‘Dump’ Luis Gil Ahead of Playoffs
What Should the Yankees Do with Anthony Volpe?
Has Anthony Volpe done enough to remain on the Yankees roster? Should be play second or third base in the MLB playoffs in place of Jazz Chisholm Jr. or Ryan McMahon.
Over his last seven games, Anthony Volpe has a home run, two doubles, eight hits, 7 RBI, and scored three runs.
In all likelihood, Jazz still has his 2B spot when he returns, but Ryan McMahon?? That’s another question.
Ryan McMahon is batting .210 this season with 10 home runs, 34 RBI, and just 66 hits.
And half of his games are in a hitters’ haven for lefties.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Get Strong Jasson Dominguez Message Ahead of MLB Playoffs
Anthony Volpe’s 2026 Season at a Glance
While Anthony Volpe’s 2026 stats don’t light the world on fire, it’s fair to note he hasn’t been given an extended runway to make a major impact, as he’s bounced between AAA and the Bigs frequently.
Across 63 games this season, Volpe is batting .253 (career-high) with 14 XBH, 26 RBI, and an OPS+ of 92 (also would be career-high).
He’s cut down on some of the strikeouts, and is still working a decent amount of walks.
Yankees fans, let me know in the comments what you think Anthony Volpe’s role should be with the team in October?
If it were me (and being clear, I’m not the GM!) I’d run Volpe out there in October at 3B. It gives the lineup right-left balance, and Anthony Volpe has at least shown a capability of putting the ball in play that Ryan McMahon hasn’t.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Sequence of the Week: Max Fried (9/15)
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: It wouldn't have been a proper Yankees-Twins series in Minnesota without a game that devolved into extra-innings madness. The Yankees failed to cash in multiple bases loaded opportunities and so missed a chance to sweep, falling farther behind the Rays in the standings. Nonetheless, the Bombers took care of business in the first two games of the series, and it is from the middle game that we pull our candidate for Sequence of the Week. We join Max Fried with two outs in the bottom of the fifth o
item.content:encoded:
It wouldn't have been a proper Yankees-Twins series in Minnesota without a game that devolved into extra-innings madness. The Yankees failed to cash in multiple bases loaded opportunities and so missed a chance to sweep, falling farther behind the Rays in the standings. Nonetheless, the Bombers took care of business in the first two games of the series, and it is from the middle game that we pull our candidate for Sequence of the Week.
We join Max Fried with two outs in the bottom of the fifth on Tuesday at Target Field. The Yankees have a 3-1 lead courtesy of a Cody Bellinger two-run homer and George Lombard Jr. RBI single. However, the Twins are threatening to cut the lead to one with Emmanuel Rodriguez on second with a two-out double. That brings the number nine hitter Austin Martin to the plate, a batter Fried absolutely wants to retire to avoid the lineup turning over with a runner in scoring position.
After going almost all fastballs the first time he faced Martin, Fried looks to steal a called first-pitch strike with a backdoor sweeper.
After seeing mostly hard stuff that moved away from him, you can understand why Martin would give up on this pitch early given how far from the strike zone it is initially aimed. Fried sweeps in a dandy on the outer half for called strike one.
Establishing that backdoor breaking ball for a called strike forces Martin to respect any pitches that start away, even those that look like balls out of the hand. This opens up a host of possibilities for Fried, including the changeup low and away for chase.
This is a pretty well-executed changeup out of the zone down and outside. It looks like it is aimed at that corner of the zone before fading away from the hitter. You can see Martin was initially tempted to chase the pitch — a product of that first pitch backdoor sweeper — before holding up for an impressively disciplined take.
With Martin taking against that last pitch away, Fried and Ali Sánchez feel that there is an opening for another backdoor sweeper.
Another decently executed pitch, just a little too low to nip the bottom of the zone for a second called strike. It is worth noting that Martin showed some willingness to offer before backing off, so that outside pitch is still open for chase opportunities.
Not wanting to fall any further behind in the count, Fried throws his first fastball of the encounter. However, unlike the four-seamers and sinkers he threw Martin in the first AB, this cutter breaks toward the hitter instead of away. Therefore, if the hitter succeeds in reading fastball spin out of the hand, a backdoor cutter that starts off the plate away should freeze Martin.
That is precisely what happens, Fried pinpointing this cutter with precision on the corner up and away. Martin leaves the bat on his shoulder, only to watch the pitch cut across the black of the plate for called strike two.
Now that he has established his fastball in the zone and has the count leverage in his favor, Fried has an opening to climb the ladder with the cutter hoping for a chase and whiff under a pitch elevated above the zone.
Even though this offering misses the top of the zone by about a foot, it's not a complete waste pitch. Fried has reset the hitter's eye level for the fastball up, which should open the door for a breaking ball down and in.
That is just what Fried's thought process is with the count full. He doesn't need to give in with a fastball with first base open, knowing that it will be very hard for Martin to lay off a breaking ball that looks like a strike out of the hand.
Now this is what you call a back-foot sweeper. The pitch looks like a strike for much of its journey toward home until the lateral sweep really seems to accelerate in the final 15 feet. It's just where you want to land a pitch like this, close enough to the strike zone to extract the chase but close enough to the batter that he is not able to pull in his hands in time to make contact.
Here's the full sequence:
Asked after the start what positives he would take away, Fried cited breaking ball command and an economical pitch count to go seven strong on just 88 pitches, the first point certainly highlighted by this sequence.
The Yankees desperately needed this start from Fried, not only to boost their chances of winning this particular game but also as a sign of continued build-up from the recurrence of his left elbow bone bruise. Fried labored in the start before this one, needing 80 pitches to complete 3.1 innings. Seeing him back to his best when it comes to pitch efficiency and damage limitation has to be encouraging as they formulate their postseason rotation plans.

item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan

The New York Yankees don't have Aaron Judge tearing it up and contending for the AL MVP this season, and while Ben Rice has been great, his odds for the award are slim due to his lackluster value defensively. But that doesn't mean the Yankees don't have someone in contention for the AL MVP award. ESPN analyst Bradford Doolit
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler gets interesting MVP update from ESPN analyst originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees don't have Aaron Judge tearing it up and contending for the AL MVP this season, and while Ben Rice has been great, his odds for the award are slim due to his lackluster value defensively.
But that doesn't mean the Yankees don't have someone in contention for the AL MVP award. ESPN analyst Bradford Doolittle does have an advanced statistic that has placed Cam Schlittler near the top of the MVP standings.
While it might still be a long shot for Schlittler to win the AL MVP, Doolittle's "AXE" rating has Schlittler second only to Yordan Alvarez, and not by much, in the AL MVP race.
Cam Schlittler is currently No. 2 in the MVP ranking by an ESPN analyst
"Front-runner: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros (146.9 AXE). Next nine: 2, Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees (143.0)," Doolittle writes.
While Doolittle noted that Schlittler has an "uphill battle" to winning the AL MVP, it's not completely out of the question just yet.
With a lack of a true runaway favorite in the AL MVP race, even with Alvarez contending for the AL Triple Crown, Schlittler's chances are much better than they normally might be.
He's been dominant this season and is the favorite, according to Doolittle, to win the AL Cy Young Award. The MVP award is significantly more difficult for Schlittler to win, and it'd take a near-perfect set of circumstances for him to have a chance at this honor.
In 31 starts this season, Schlittler has a 1.95 ERA and 7.1 bWAR. To win the AL MVP, he'd need to make at least one more start, likely a lengthy one without allowing a run, and to take the MLB ERA title, not just the AL ERA title.
Even if he were to pitch a perfect game in his final start of the year, he would need two other things to happen to win this AL MVP award.
The first would be for Alvarez to lose the Triple Crown while the Astros miss out on the playoffs. The other would be for Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays to have a terrible final few games of the year and drop the Rays out of the AL East lead.
All in all, it's nearly impossible for Schlittler to end the 2026 season as the AL MVP. But considering that pitchers never have a chance for this award, the fact that Doolittle is even willing to name him as a candidate is a testament to how great he's been this season.

item.dc:creator: TJ French
item.description: The New York Yankees have lots of decisions to make ahead of their pursuit for a World Series crown. After the Yankees clinched a postseason berth recently, as expected, it’s time to start thinking about who the Yankees could roll out in their 26-man October roster. One fringe player is outfielder Jasson Dominguez, and recently, FanSided.com’s Jake Elman sent a strong message regarding Dominguez’s roster chances. More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision Wi
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have lots of decisions to make ahead of their pursuit for a World Series crown.
After the Yankees clinched a postseason berth recently, as expected, it’s time to start thinking about who the Yankees could roll out in their 26-man October roster.
One fringe player is outfielder Jasson Dominguez, and recently, FanSided.com’s Jake Elman sent a strong message regarding Dominguez’s roster chances.
More MLB on Heavy: New York Yankees Urged to Make Bold Paul Goldschmidt Decision
Will Jasson Dominguez Make Yankees Playoff Roster?
Right now, for the Yankees, the biggest storyline on the postseason roster front is Aaron Judge.
Judge has noted that he’s healthy after exiting a recent game against the Twins, but he’s the Yankees’ crown jewel.
Anywho, back to Jasson Dominguez, who is 100% a fringe roster candidate headed into October.
Elman recently noted Dominguez as a player who may be dumped from the Yankees’ postseason roster, and he wrote:
“The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder. Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.”
More MLB on Heavy: Former Chicago Cubs Player Demoted by New MLB Team
Jasson Dominguez’s 2026 Season
Jasson Dominguez was expected to take a leap in his development this season as the Yankees’ top backup outfielder, but he’s bounced back between the Bigs and minors all season due to inconsistent performance up in the big leagues.
Across 57 games played this season, Dominguez has batted just .225 with a negative bWAR, six home runs, 12 doubles, and an OPS+ of 75.
Those statistics aren’t very good.
Yankees fans, what would you do with Jasson Dominguez as the MLB playoffs approach? Would he be on your roster as a backup outfielder/pinch-runner?
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Quietly Announce Roster News on 26-Year-Old Pitcher

Judge comenzó a sentir la molestia después de su primer turno al bate, pero permaneció varios innings en el terreno. Después de conversar con Aaron Boone, decidió no continuar y Heliot Ramos tomó su lugar como bateador emergente y jardinero derecho.
- LEER MÁS: Roberto Clemente Day: así fueron los homenajes que marcaron la jornada

Las primeras señales resultaron tranquilizadoras. Judge declaró que no espera necesitar estudios de imágenes y considera que la salida fue una medida preventiva para evitar que la molestia se convierta en una lesión más importante.
Los Yankees aprovecharán el día de descanso para realizar tratamiento y evaluar su evolución antes de comenzar la serie contra Arizona Diamondbacks. Boone no descartó que pueda regresar rápidamente, aunque el club evitará acelerar su recuperación.

item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan

This upcoming offseason, the New York Yankees are going to have a few big decisions to make. One of the biggest question marks will revolve around Jazz Chisholm Jr. The All-Star second baseman is set to be a free agent, and his future is very much up in the air. While the Yankees could bring him back, it would not be a
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. broke out at wrong time amid 2026 disappointment originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
This upcoming offseason, the New York Yankees are going to have a few big decisions to make. One of the biggest question marks will revolve around Jazz Chisholm Jr.
The All-Star second baseman is set to be a free agent, and his future is very much up in the air. While the Yankees could bring him back, it would not be a surprise if he left for a new team this offseason.
Unfortunately for Chisholm, this is not a good time for him to hit the open market. As CBS Sports' Matt Snyder noted, Chisholm's 2025 breakout came a year too early, as his 2026 letdown is likely to tank his free-agent value this offseason.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. likely to face FA challenge amid letdown season
"He's one year late on the ideal time to hit free agency," Snyder writes. "... There's still plenty of potential to dream on, and he won't have trouble finding good offers heading towards his age-29 season, but this season has been a definitive step backward."
Chisholm's free agent value has dropped considerably this offseason, as his production has gone from All-Star to just an above-average player.
He had 4.1 bWAR in 130 games last season. This year for the Yankees, he has 1.4 bWAR in 134 games. It's a clear step in the wrong direction, and it will have a big impact on his free agency.
He had 31 homers and 31 stolen bases last season. This year he has just 19 homers, although his 40 stolen bases have helped make up for the lackluster homer numbers.
But the most alarming issue for Chisholm is that his 122 OPS+ and .813 OPS from a year ago have dropped considerably to a 98 OPS+ and .715 OPS.
If Chisholm had hit the open market after his 2025 season a year ago, he would've been looking at a deal that could've gotten close to $30 million or more per-year.
Now, it might be difficult for Chisholm to hit that number, even as a power-hitting, base-stealing infielder who is only going to be heading into his age-29 season.
Chisholm will still likely get a decent deal on the open market. Just compared to what kind of offers he'd receive had he been a free agent after last season, it's looking likely to be an underwhelming free agency for Chisholm this year.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] 4 Things We Learned from Clarke Schmidt's 2026 Debut in Yankees' 5-4 Extra Innings Loss vs. Twins
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually. Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive. The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnes
item.content:encoded:
On the offensive front, the New York Yankees have a lot to worry about. Pitching-wise, things are okay — more than okay, actually.
Despite a lackluster trade deadline in which general manager Brian Cashman failed to add any relievers, the team bolstered its pitching depth in the weeks that followed. They lucked out by adding John Schreiber, which was essentially a salary dump for the Kansas City Royals, and Clarke Schmidt coming off the IL is another positive.
The Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon was an ugly one they needed, and Minnesota's walk-off left a bad taste, while Aaron Judge had another injury scare. But it was another stellar day for the pen, outside of David Bednar letting up two leads in extras. Schmidt is one reason to look forward to what the pen could be in October, and even if he has a little more rust to knock off, there are a few things to be excited about.
Giving length
Schmidt isn't built up, but he should be good to give a little more than an inning at a time as a reliever. While he only pitched 2/3 innings in his return to the mound, it's clear the Yankees are building Schmidt up to go multiple innings. In three of his five rehab starts, he pitched more than one inning. In two of them, he pitched two innings.
Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick have clearly been overworked. Somebody like Schmidt lightens their load, and soon another starter, Ryan Weathers, will join the bullpen.
More strikeout stuff in the bullpen
The Yankees have desperately needed strikeout stuff, especially in the middle innings. The Yankees have guys who can generate whiffs in Bednar, Blackburn, and Headrick, but that's missing if a starter comes out early. Schmidt gives them that. He struck out two batters in his debut, and despite allowing two hits, he navigated through it because of the whiffs.
Schmidt also showed strikeout stuff in his rehab start. He struck out 11 batters in seven innings. He hasn't had a full season since 2023, but in 2024 and 2025 combined, the veteran hurler had a 9.11 K/9. That should play in October.
No more sweeper?
The sweeper was Schmidt's second-most-used pitch in 2024. It was his third-most-used pitch in 2023. Against the Minnesota Twins, he didn't throw it once. It could be a pitch he's throwing away.
It would be a surprise if he did that, though. Batters hit .210 off it and struck out 33.8% of the time against it in 2024. In 2025, they hit .125 off the sweeper. They struck out 35.8% of the time against it. It's something to look to in future outings.
Potential trade bait
You can never have too much pitching, and if there is one thing the 2026 Yankees understand full well, it's that pitching depth is paramount. It's how they navigated the season.
That said, Schmidt has one year left after this season. The Yankees may want to sell high on him if they don't plan on bringing him back. The rotation should be full again next year, and if they need pitching depth, they have Ryan Weathers and Will Warren.
This season could be a showcase of sorts for Schmidt. The veteran showing he can finish out the season could be a selling point in the winter.
Chances are, Schmidt won't be able to start next year anyway, and if he does, he won't have a full workload since he needs to build back up. The last time he pitched more than 150 innings was in 2023. That said, the Yankees could use this as an opportunity to deal an oft-injured pitcher and fill another area of need.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [NBC Sports] Were we wrong about Yankees rookie outfielder Spencer Jones?
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski
item.description: When Yankees’ outfielder Spencer Jones made his MLB debut back in May, many people, including myself, were skeptical that his approach would work at the MLB level. While he had succeeded in the minors, he was older than most of his opponents and had displayed real issues with contact and strikeouts. It didn’t seem like a profile that would translate well and, early on, that was proven to be correct. In his first 82 plate appearances, Jones hit .233 with a 41.5% strikeout rate, a 21% swinging str
item.content:encoded:
When Yankees’ outfielder Spencer Jones made his MLB debut back in May, many people, including myself, were skeptical that his approach would work at the MLB level. While he had succeeded in the minors, he was older than most of his opponents and had displayed real issues with contact and strikeouts. It didn’t seem like a profile that would translate well and, early on, that was proven to be correct.
In his first 82 plate appearances, Jones hit .233 with a 41.5% strikeout rate, a 21% swinging strike rate, and well below-average contact rates and zone contact rates. The Yankees demoted him to Triple-A at the beginning of July, and it seemed like he may not be part of the team’s plans moving forward.
Yet, since coming back up on July 22nd, Jones is hitting .261/.326/.472 with eight home runs, 30 RBI, and eight steals. That has come with a 33.5% strikeout rate and a 19.5% swinging strike rate, but also a 77% zone contact rate that is better than many expected him to produce. So is this sustainable? Can Jones keep producing at this level with his strikeout rates and swinging strike rates as elevated as they are?
To answer that question, I not only went to the data, but I watched the vast majority of his at-bats since July 22nd, thanks, in huge part, to my buddy Nick Pollack, who gave me access to a pitcher database where you can watch specific at-bats. We don’t have to tell Nick that I watched it for a hitter instead of a pitcher. Regardless, this article is now a combination of what the data and my own eyes tell me about whether or not my Spencer Jones skepticism was off base and if he can be a true difference-maker for the Yankees during his career.
The Results Don’t Lie - He Hits the Ball Incredibly Hard
We have to start with the results because if they weren’t what they are, nobody would be asking this question. We already talked about Jones’ stat line and his contact rate since returning to the Yankees’ roster. We should also note that he has a 19.4% barrel rate, 51.5% hard-hit rate, and 77 mph bat speed in his 179 plate appearances. All of that is beyond elite. No matter where he makes contact with the ball (except maybe up-and-in), he’s crushing it.
Despite also having a .362 BABIP over this stretch, Jones is not getting lucky, according to Statcast, which gives him a .266 xBA and a .520 xSLG. At bare minimum, it means that Jones’ performance is not obviously flukey based on batted ball data. His .362 BABIP may regress closer to the league average of .290 over this stretch, but the rest of the results aren’t screaming red flags. Which means we can start digging into the details with a slight lean towards an optimistic view on Jones.
Jones Crushes Fastballs But Can He Handle Other Pitches?
As you might expect from a player with Jones’ raw power, he handles fastballs, both four-seamers and sinkers, exceptionally well. Heading into Wednesday’s game against the Twins, Jones had a .936 OPS since July 22nd against four-seamers, with a 96.0 mph average exit velocity, 22.7% barrel rate, and 54.5% hard-hit rate. That’s genuinely elite contact quality. His expected batting average against four-seamers was .426, which was notably higher than his .317 actual average, which supports that he has been hitting four-seamers as well as you could expect a hitter to.
In a much smaller sample size, Jones’ sinker results look even better, with a 1.103 OPS, 99 mph average exit velocity, and 66.7% hard-hit rate. Of course, he has only seen 67 sinkers, so we need to take that with a grain of salt, but it’s notable that both the fastball and sinker feature the lowest swinging strike rates for Jones among all of the pitches he has faced regularly (he didn’t face enough splitters for me to include the data).
| Pitch Type | Pitches Seen | BA | OPS | SwStr% | Avg Exit Velo | Hard-Hit% | Balls In Play | Expected BA (xBA) |
| Four-seam | 288 | 0.317 | 0.936 | 13.5% | 96.0 | 54.5% | 44 | 0.426 |
| Changeup | 103 | 0.160 | 0.512 | 31.1% | 89.8 | 41.7% | 12 | 0.398 |
| Slider | 90 | 0.227 | 0.655 | 25.6% | 94.1 | 46.2% | 13 | 0.402 |
| Sinker | 67 | 0.286 | 1.103 | 10.4% | 99.0 | 66.7% | 9 | 0.595 |
| Curveball | 49 | 0.100 | 0.200 | 26.5% | 88.3 | 50.0% | 6 | 0.304 |
| Sweeper | 34 | 0.625 | 1.625 | 17.6% | 88.7 | 42.9% | 7 | 0.433 |
As you can see from the pitch samples, again, before Wednesday’s game, Jones has seen four-seamers nearly three times as often as any other single pitch. That’s a curious decision from pitchers given the amount of damage he does against them, but that’s a conversation for another time.
We can also notice from the chart that Jones’ hard-hit rate is genuinely strong against all pitch types. However, the swinging strike rate gets significantly worse, particularly on changeups, where Jones has a 31.1% mark. Considering he has seen over 100 changeups, that is likely not a small-sample-size data error; Jones really struggles against changeups. Similarly, in a much smaller sample size, he has struggled to make contact with curveballs, but has hit them hard, so this all jives pretty cleanly with the idea that Jones has tons of power in his bat, but struggles to make consistent contact. If he were to start seeing far fewer four-seamers, how would he handle that?
Contact Rate and Swing Decisions Concerns
Earlier, I mentioned that Jones’ 77% zone contact rate over this stretch was far better than I expected him to produce. While that’s true, we also need to highlight that the MLB average zone contact rate over the same sample size is 87.1%. Similarly, his 19.5% swinging strike rate is well above the 10.8% league average, and his 64% contact rate overall is below the league average of 77.4%. No matter which way you slice it, Jones is far below the league average when it comes to his contact ability, even when he’s producing such elite results.
In fact, over this stretch, only Munetaka Murakami and Esmerlyn Valdez have a lower contact rate among the 168 qualified hitters in all of baseball. Jones ranks 166th out of 168 qualified hitters in contact rate despite his scorching results at the plate. Similarly, his 77% zone contact rate, which we lauded, ranks 161st out of 168 qualified hitters.
In particular, he seems to have a weakness up in the zone and particularly up-and-away. As you can see in the Statcast zone breakdowns below, Jones whiffs more at the top of the zone than anywhere else, and he produces poor batted ball results at the top of the zone. That might be why he sees so many fastballs, but if pitchers aren’t able to locate successfully up in the zone, Jones can punish pitches in the middle of the zone and also low. However, these charts seem to show some real weak points where pitchers could attack the rookie.
Some of Jones’ contact concerns come down to swing decisions. Jones has a chase rate of 37.9% over this stretch, which is the 39th-most among the same 168 qualified hitters. Jones also sees his chase rate climb as he gets deeper into the count. It’s 36.6% when he’s ahead in the count, 38.7% when he’s in an even count, and 40.2% when he’s behind in the count. All of that is compared to the league average chase rate over the same sample size of 33.2%. While it’s natural for hitters to expand the zone more to try and protect the plate in two-strike counts, we have to acknowledge that Jones expands the zone far more than average in all counts.
Part of that is aggression. He has a 53.7% swing rate over this stretch that ranks 23rd among the same batch of qualified hitters. The league average swing rate is 47.6%. Yet, swinging more often makes sense for Jones. We’ve seen plenty of hitters with poor contact profiles swing more often because it gives them more chances to make contact and do damage. That aggression is not necessarily a negative for him so long as it results in early swing and misses that give him extra chances to hit and not weak contact that ends an at-bat.
That might also be why Jones gets even MORE aggressive with runners in scoring position, where his swing rate increases from 51.2% to 59.5%, and his chase rate climbs from 36.6% to 44.4%. When you pair that with the fact that his contact rate and swinging-strike rate are both also worse with runners in scoring position, you’d think Jones struggles there, but he actually entered Wednesday’s game with a .378 batting average and 1.158 OPS with runners in scoring position. That’s compared to a .211 average and .657 OPS with the bases empty. His aggression in those situations has potentially been the cause of his success.
This also isn’t luck. He may be getting overly aggressive with runners in scoring position and expanding the zone a lot, but when he puts the ball in play in these spots, he’s genuinely crushing it. He has three home runs in these situations, and all three were balls that were 104.6 mph or harder. He has singles that registered 105.9 mph, 102.2 mph, and 108.5 mph. In fact, he has only one poorly hit base hit with runners in scoring position over this whole sample, which was a 53.1 mph roller with a -28° launch angle that found a hole for a single.
So, yes, his contact rates and swing decisions are not good. But also, no, that has not been hurting his overall performance.
He Is Willing to Make Two-Strike Adjustments
Another factor that points towards Jones’ results being genuine is that he has shown the desire to change his approach in two-strike counts. That’s good because he gets into a lot of them. Since July 22nd, 60% of Jones’ plate appearances reach a two-strike count. The league average is 52.7%. We obviously mentioned his aggression earlier on in this article, and we know that Jones swings and misses a lot, so it makes sense that he would get behind in the count often.
Yet, when his aggression works for him, it works in impressive ways.
In the 40% of plate appearances where Jones avoids a two-strike count, he has hit .460 with a 1.341 OPS and a 50.8% hard-hit rate. Now, we need to note that a 1.341 OPS in 63 at-bats is an extreme number that we should expect to come back down to earth as the sample grows. That’s not because Jones is bad, but because numbers this high rarely hold at that level over a larger sample size.
Now, when Jones does get into two-strike counts, his bat speed, swing length, and swing tilt are all essentially unchanged, which means he’s not making any glaring mechanical changes depending on the count. However, his attack angle, which measures the vertical angle of the sweet spot of the bat when it passes through the contact point, is over two degrees flatter in two-strike counts. That may be a small sample size fluke, but it also may be evidence that Jones is trying to create a flatter bat path when he gets behind in the count.
Another data point that supports that notion is that Jones’ best contact rate comes in two-strike counts. Now, it’s still just 71.3%, and his swinging strike rate in two-strike counts remains 16%, but those are noticeable improvements from what he’s doing in other counts. This supports the idea that he is tightening up his swing and focusing on making contact in these situations. That contact has produced just a .481 OPS, which is a huge gap of about .860 points between his two-strike and non-two-strike OPS; however, we can’t drag a guy for not making enough contact and then also drag him when he changes his swing to protect the plate and make more contact. It’s clear that Jones has the mature understanding that he needs to change his approach with two strikes, and that points to continued development from him in the future.
Is On the Extreme End of a Common Profile
In order to see which hitters Jones most closely resembles, I sorted by hitters who were in both the top quartile in swinging strike rate (negatively), zone contact rate (negatively), and the top quartile in hard-hit rate (positively). I found 33 hitters who have similar types of profiles to Spencer Jones. A lot of them are names you’d likely have imagined, and even after I removed a few of them because they either didn’t hit the ball hard enough or made too much contact in the zone, we had an intriguing list to compare to.
| Player | SwStr% | Hard-Hit% | Zone Contact% |
| Esmerlyn Valdez | 14.9% | 49.3% | 71.3% |
| Munetaka Murakami | 15.9% | 57.1% | 71.3% |
| Luke Raley | 20.6% | 47.1% | 76.9% |
| Spencer Jones | 19.5% | 54.3% | 77.0% |
| Nick Kurtz | 14.1% | 57.3% | 77.5% |
| Garrett Mitchell | 14.5% | 53.1% | 80.0% |
| Griffin Conine | 16.9% | 49.7% | 80.1% |
| Oneil Cruz | 14.5% | 55.4% | 80.2% |
| Kyle Stowers | 17.5% | 56.5% | 82.1% |
| Kyle Schwarber | 13.3% | 49.9% | 82.3% |
| Jordan Walker | 15.3% | 48.9% | 82.6% |
| Jake Burger | 16.5% | 46.3% | 82.8% |
| Corey Seager | 14.9% | 48.4% | 84.3% |
| Henry Bolte | 15.1% | 47.8% | 85.3% |
| Heliot Ramos | 13.2% | 50.4% | 86.2% |
| Jac Caglianone | 14.9% | 54.5% | 87.2% |
As you can see, even from this list of outliers, Jones is an outlier himself. He has the 4th-lowest zone contact rate (77%) in the entire 33-player group, basically tied with Luke Raley. Only Esmerlyn Valdez and Munetaka Murakami have been worse among this group. Both of those two hitters had better swinging-strike rates than Jones, whose swinging strike rate is second-highest on this list, trailing only Raley. Of course, on the flip side, only five hitters in the 33-hitter sample had a higher hard-hit rate than Jones, which puts him as a positive outlier too. All of which is to say that Jones, even during his recent hot streak, has proven to swing and miss an extreme amount, both overall and in the zone, but also hit the ball incredibly hard when he does make contact.
I found the comparisons to Esmerlyn Valdez and Munetaka Murakami to be interesting because both have proven to be incredibly streaky this season.
In his first 74 games of the season, Murakami hit .244/.382/.553 with 24 home runs and 51 RBI. That came with a 20.1% barrel rate and 60.4% hard-hit rate. He was among the most elite power hitters in the game. That’s also a 344 plate appearance sample, so almost double Jones’ 179 plate appearances. Murakami’s 16.3% swinging strike rate was better than Jones’ mark by over 3%; however, Murakami had a far worse 70.3% zone contact rate and a slightly worse 60.4% contact rate.
It appears that his hamstring injury, or poor contact rates, caught up with Murakami, who has hit .131/.277/.301 with seven home runs and a 42% strikeout rate in 184 plate appearances since August 1st. His zone contact rate is an identical 70.4% over that stretch, and his contact rate fell to 59.2%. It’s unlikely that Jones would experience that kind of regression since his zone contact issues are not as pronounced as Murakami’s.
The same could maybe be said for Valdez, who was also called back up after a rough first MLB sample size, and hit .310/.406/.716 with 12 home runs and 32 RBI in his first 138 plate appearances from June 22nd on. Remember that this sample size for Jones is 179 plate appearances, so Valdez wasn’t as hot for as long, but it’s a closer gap than Murakami. Valdez also, like Murakami, scorched the ball with a 24.7% barrel rate and 51% hard-hit rate, but also posted a 73% zone contact rate and 66% contact rate overall. Interestingly, that means Valdez had a better swinging strike rate and overall contact rate than Jones over his sample size; however, Valdez also had more issues with contact in the zone.
In 123 plate appearances since August 1st, Valdez has hit .178/.317/.317 with three home runs and a 41.5% strikeout rate. Even though his profile is more similar to Jones’ than Murakami’s, I still don’t think it’s quite a fair comparison because Jones has had better zone contact rates, so he may not have regression hit him as hard as those two players did.
So who does Jones most closely resemble?
That hard truth is that the answer is really “Nobody.” Jones combines three separate extremes at the same time, which appears to be rare when you look at the hitters on this list. Most of these hitters, who are already elite power hitters with some contact concerns, have two extreme outcomes but are closer to league average in a third. For example, Nick Kurtz has a near-identical zone contact rate to Jones and only slightly better hard-hit rates, but a significantly better swinging strike rate. Kyle Stowers has a hard-hit rate that resembles Jones’ and also has an elevated swinging strike rate, but both of those marks are better than Jones’, and Stowers also has a 5% better zone contact rate.
Jones’ basic archetype of being a high-whiff, big-power hitter isn’t rare, but when factoring in zone contact, he struggles to make contact on pitches he should be able to handle at a rate that’s similar to almost no other hitter who also hits the ball this hard. Your closest comparison might be Griffin Conine or maybe Luke Raley with more pop and athleticism (meaning, he can actually play defense).
We need to be clear that this isn’t who Jones WILL BE. He’s 25 years old, so there is a world where he continues to improve and adjust to MLB pitching and comes closer to an Oneil Cruz type of profile; although, even that would require a 5% decrease in swinging strike rate. He should also note that Cruz has a career slash line of .241/.320/.436, so even if we’re saying the contact profile for Jones could grow into becoming more than Cruz, that would likely still result in a far lower batting average over a full season.
Final Takeaway
At the end of the day, Spencer Jones is a truly unique player. We’ve really yet to see somebody who truly resembles his profile as closely as we’d like. However, we can say that he’s clearly better than I, and many others, thought he’d be at the MLB level. That needs to be said directly and outright if we’re being honest in our takeaways from this research. I thought his contact profile would be so poor that he would rarely be able to make enough useful contact to be an MLB regular. I underestimated the quality of contact that he is able to make when he does square up the ball.
However, I do maintain my belief that contact rate wins out in the end. I’ve just seen it too many times over all my years playing, watching, and writing about baseball. It’s nearly impossible for a player to maintain consistent, year-after-year production with bottom-tier contact rates. Major League pitchers are simply too good, and they find a way to exploit it.
That being said, I think it’s fair to come away from this believing that Jones is an MLB regular. He possesses good speed and a solid enough defensive profile that I think you can play him as one of your regular outfielders. He has also hit left-handers well enough in a small sample size that you may not need to force a strong-side platoon on him. However, I think there’s also a strong argument that we’re seeing the best stretch he’s going to have. Considering that stretch has a .261/.326/.472 slash line, we might see Jones settle in as a .240 type of hitter.
There are plenty of those types of hitters who are impactful MLB players: Oneil Cruz, Kyle Schwarber, Max Muncy, Hunter Goodman, etc. Jones will need to continue to make strides to get near that tier of player, but he’s showing that it may not be as impossible as I had believed. Although maybe still a little improbable.

item.content:encoded:
Perhaps Pete Alonso will get a standing ovation if he slugs a game-tying home run off David Bednar next week.
The Orioles first baseman, who received a hero’s welcome in his return to Flushing this week, made a rather odd Yankees reference while thanking Mets fans for the love they showered him with this week.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
“I am beyond thankful for all the support and it was really fun to play,” Alonso said after homering in the Orioles’ 7-1 win over the Mets on Wednesday at Citi Field to complete a three-game sweep.
“I feel like New York will always be a place where it feels like homecoming – it doesn’t matter whether it’s here or at Yankee Stadium. The whole city of New York is meaningful to us.”
It’s certainly understandable that Alonso would feel the love at Citi Field from Mets fans since it would appear most team supporters wish the team did not leave him leave.
There isn’t that history with the Yankees, though, and he’s performed quite well against them in his career.
Alonso, spanning his seven seasons with the Mets and this first with the AL East rival Orioles, owns a career .253/.333/.558 slash line with 14 homers and 35 RBIs in his career against the Bronx Bombers.
At Yankee Stadium, Alonso has hit .247/.312/.600 with nine homers and 21 RBIs in 23 games.
Alonso went 5-for-14 with two solo homers in the Yankees’ four-game sweep in The Bronx from May 1-4 this year.
With just 42 games against the Yankees under his belt, the first baseman is statistically averaging a homer in every three-game set and five RBIs every six games.
When he and the Orioles visit Yankee Stadium for a season-ending series next weekend, it’s possible it could matter for both teams.
The Yankees are not likely to win the AL East but they could be in the race still dependent on how next week’s four-game set with the Rays plays out in The Bronx.
They also could be battling the Red Sox, who they lead by six games while owning the tiebreaker, for the top wild-card spot.
The Orioles (75-78) are 2 1/2 games out of the third and final Wild Card spot and would need to pass three teams to return to the postseason for the first time since 2024.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Carlos Rodon sets franchise record
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: MLB has witnessed an impressive run from New York Yankees left-hander Carlos Rodon, who is putting together one of the most consistent stretches in franchise history. The 33-year-old Rodon has not allowed more than three runs in 25 consecutive starts, establishing the longest such streak in Yankees franchise history. His run is also tied for the sixth-longest streak in MLB history, putting his recent performances among the most remarkable stretches by a pitcher. A historic run on the mound Oct 1
item.content:encoded:
MLB has witnessed an impressive run from New York Yankees left-hander Carlos Rodon, who is putting together one of the most consistent stretches in franchise history.
The 33-year-old Rodon has not allowed more than three runs in 25 consecutive starts, establishing the longest such streak in Yankees franchise history. His run is also tied for the sixth-longest streak in MLB history, putting his recent performances among the most remarkable stretches by a pitcher.
A historic run on the mound
Oct 1, 2025; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Carlos Rodon (55) looks on after leaving the game during the seventh inning against the Boston Red Sox during game two of the Wildcard round for the 2025 MLB playoffs at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Rodon's latest outing continued that consistency. He allowed two earned runs on four hits while striking out five over six innings against the Minnesota Twins. Despite another solid performance from their starter, the Yankees ultimately fell 5-4 to Minnesota in a marathon 13-inning game.
Rodon's streak dates back to Aug. 1, 2025, when he surrendered four runs over 4.2 innings against the Miami Marlins. Since then, he has managed to keep opposing offenses from scoring more than three runs in every regular-season start.
Strong season for the Yankees lefty
Rodon has also delivered strong numbers throughout the 2026 campaign. He is 6-3 with a 2.95 ERA through 15 starts, giving him his lowest ERA since the 2022 season. That year, while pitching for the San Francisco Giants, Rodon recorded a 2.88 ERA.
His consistency has been particularly valuable as the Yankees navigate the final stretch of the regular season. New York currently holds an 11-game lead at the top of the American League Wild Card standings with fewer than two weeks remaining in the MLB regular season.
The Yankees are still chasing the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East, sitting 4.5 games behind the division leaders. Their next challenge comes Friday, when they begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks.
With the postseason approaching, Rodon's historic streak gives the Yankees another dependable arm as they look to finish the regular season strong.

item.content:encoded:
Ryan McMahon's tenure with the New York Yankees hasn't gone as planned. He has certainly been a strong fielder at third base (though not as exceptional as he was sold), but his bat has been anemic by any metric. So much so that after going 0-for-6 with four strikeouts on Wednesday, he has officially joined similar territory as a number of infamous Yankees who underperformed during their time in pinstripes.
As pointed out by Jack Fungo on X, McMahon has a 80 wRC+ in 162 games since being acquired by the Yankees at the 2025 trade deadline. That is a lower mark than DJ LeMahieu's final season with the Yankees when he got released, Josh Donaldson's career in the Bronx, Joey Gallo's time with the Yankees, Isiah Kiner-Falefa's 2023 season and Anthony Volpe's 2025 season.
Ryan McMahon's Yankees company proves the DFA bells are tolling
This isn't great company to be in for McMahon. To put things in perspective, McMahon is 20 points below the league average of 100 for wRC+. On the season, McMahon has hit 10 home runs, has driven in 34 RBI and sports a .210/.275/.346 slash line with a .621 OPS.
McMahon had some solid offensive years with the Colorado Rockies in his career, but his home splits were always much better due to his numbers at Coors Field being inflated as a result of the high altitude. The writing appeared to be on the wall for McMahon before he switched cities.
But the Yankees traded for McMahon because they were desperate for a third baseman last year. They also landed Amed Rosario to platoon with McMahon at the hot corner. Neither has stepped up to claim the job on an everyday basis, though Rosario's bat has been markedly better lately (.348 average in his last seven sporadically placed games).
Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason. There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahonunder contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees, and his time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] 25 starts later, Carlos Rodón has made the Yankees' October call uncomfortable
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: There is a point where a nice stretch stops being a nice stretch. Carlos Rodón has crossed that line for the Yankees. Rodón gave them six innings, two earned runs and five strikeouts on Wednesday in Minnesota. The 5-4 loss took some shine off the afternoon, but his start extended a run that is getting hard to brush aside: 25 straight outings with no more than three runs allowed and no more than one homer surrendered. item.content:encoded:
There is a point where a nice stretch stops being a nice stretch. Carlos Rodón has crossed that line for the Yankees.
Rodón gave them six innings, two earned runs and five strikeouts on Wednesday in Minnesota. The 5-4 loss took some shine off the afternoon, but his start extended a run that is getting hard to brush aside: 25 straight outings with no more than three runs allowed and no more than one homer surrendered.
He does not have to start Game 1. Max Fried and Cam Schlittler have been excellent, and October is not a participation trophy for everybody who had a good September. The rotation conversation cannot be handled with old assumptions anymore.
The Yankees have a real surplus of starters who can make a case. It is a good issue to have, but the first series is short and the opponent decides who gets the ball after the opener.
The Yankees have to count the whole body of work
Rodón’s recent run is not built on smoke. He has kept the ball in the yard, limited crooked innings, and worked deep enough into games to spare the bullpen. Wednesday was not perfect, with three walks and 102 pitches, yet he gave New York a clean six-inning start while the game was still there for the taking.
October asks for exactly that kind of start. Nobody needs a masterpiece every time; they need someone who can keep a game in the middle innings without handing the other dugout a free runway.
I would not overreact to one loss in Minneapolis. I would react to the 25-start sample, because it now carries real weight in the Yankees’ season.
Carlos Rodón has earned a real say in October
The reasonable answer may be matchups. A left-handed lineup could push Rodón up the board, while a series schedule might make a different order cleaner. Fine. The Yankees should use every edge they can find.
What they should not do is treat Rodón like the interchangeable third or fourth starter just because that was easier to say months ago. His work has made the pecking order less tidy. Good pitchers tend to do that.
The rotation debate is not settled, and it should not be. Rodón has made sure it will be an actual decision instead of a formality.
More about:New York Yankees
