item.content:encoded:
For their sake, the New York Yankees better hope that superstar outfielder Aaron Judge’s newest injury is only a minor setback.
Judge left Wednesday’s extra-inning loss to the Twins with lower leg tightness, immediately raising concerns among fans that he’ll miss the Yankees’ first playoff series. New York entered play on Sept. 17 in firm control of the AL’s top Wild Card seed, putting them on track to host the No. 5 Red Sox in the first round.
If Judge can’t go when the playoffs begin on Sept. 29, then he won’t be the only notable contributor not in uniform during the Wild Card Series. Each team gets 26 players for their playoff rosters, but no more than 13 pitchers. Some clubs opt for 14 position players and 12 pitchers, though we personally prefer a 13-and-13 balance. Additionally, teams can adjust their rosters between series, and obviously they can replace an injured player if needed.
For this list, we’re only including players who are healthy and active as of Sept. 17. In other words, that means Trent Grisham, Giancarlo Stanton, and Ryan Weathers are among those who didn’t qualify. We’ve also omitted Judge because the Yankees haven’t announced the severity of his left leg injury.
Jasson Domínguez, OF
The writing has long been on the wall for Domínguez, who was recently demoted to Triple-A amid another disappointing season. Even if Judge potentially misses the Wild Card Round, it’s difficult to envision the 23-year-old Domínguez returning as a backup outfielder.
Frankly, the entire situation is unfortunate, because neither Domínguez’s talent nor his work ethic has been the issue. He’s always earned rave reviews for his maturity and overall attitude, but injuries — most notably to his elbow and shoulder — have seemingly sapped him of his once-potent power stroke.
Luis Gil, P
Gil has had an odd career, winning AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 despite debuting three years earlier. Injuries have limited him to a 3.92 ERA over 80.1 innings since the start of 2025, and he recently moved to the bullpen. We’ll see whether the Yankees view the 28-year-old as a long-term reliever, or if they’d bring him to spring training as a starter.
But for now, Gil is on the roster bubble, and we don’t expect him to crack the 26-man playoff squad. Clarke Schmidt’s return gives the Yankees another depth arm, and Gil hasn’t shown that he’s worth carrying on a limited staff. That said, we imagine he’d be among the first names called if injuries strike his teammates.
Paul Goldschmidt, 1B/DH
Goldschmidt turned 39 last week, and it’s unclear whether he’s in the final weeks of a likely Hall of Fame career. He’s totaled 65.3 bWAR, and the majority of the 142 players above him are already in the Hall of Fame or will be when they’re eligible.
Let’s get back to the present. Goldschmidt is hitting just .239 with a .680 OPS in 103 second-half plate appearances, and he’s only capable of playing first or DHing. Ben Rice fills both roles, and Cody Bellinger can also play first if needed.
The one thing potentially working in Goldschmidt’s favor is his .313 average and 1.006 OPS against lefties, but that’s not enough to warrant a roster spot in our eyes. Sorry, Goldy. At least you’d finally earn a World Series ring if the Yankees finish the job.
Will Warren, SP
This might come as a surprise, given that we included Warren in our most recent playoff roster projection. But the more that we think about things, Schmidt’s return feels like a significant blow to Warren’s chances of pitching in October. Do the Yankees really need two long relievers capable of eating up innings if the starter leaves early?
We initially had veteran swingman Ryan Yarbrough in this spot, though he might have the advantage as a left-handed reliever.. He also has a 2.91 ERA in 21.2 second-half innings and has since recovered from a lingering right oblique problem.

item.content:encoded:
The schedule may have done the New York Yankees a tiny favor in regards to what happens next after Aaron Judge left Wednesday's game in Minnesota with an injury.
The Yankees are off on Thursday before returning to action Friday, so it's a built-in rest day of sorts.
It also means, though, that Yankees fans waiting for a quick turnaround on another Judge update may have to be patient. There's less likelihood of additional news emerging on Thursday when the Yankees don't have a game to play.
The Yankees are on the road and won't play again until Friday night in Arizona against the Diamondbacks. That game will begin at what is 9:40 p.m. ET back in the Bronx.
Aaron Judge Injury: What Happened?
Judge was lifted for a pinch-hitter during the Yankees' 5-4 loss to the Twins on Wednesday.
Heliot Ramos entered to take that sixth-inning at bat in place of Judge.
Judge said after the game that he felt stiffness in his lower right leg in the first inning. He struck out in his first two at bats and played the field as well before the decision was made to get him out of the game.
"I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch," Judge said after the game, via MLB.com. "But kind of talking it over, I thought it'd be the right move to come out, so I don't cost the team on the field or cost the team on the basepath."
MLB.com's Patrick Donnelly wrote after the game that Judge is going to receive "extensive treatment over the next 48 hours."
Judge added after the game that he couldn't pinpoint a specific moment that the injury may have occurred. He noted that the ramp up in his return from the rib injury that kept him out for more than three months might explain this — "Once you start ramping up again, things pop up, and that's where we've been," Judge said.
What's Next for Aaron Judge?
The Yankees aren't jumping to conclusions.
"We're not going to speculate one way or the other," manager Aaron Boone told reporters after Wednesday's game. "We'll just see how he responds."
It's not going to be an easy finishing run for the Yankees.
The three-game series in Arizona comes against a Diamondbacks team that has a fighting chance to claim the National League's final Wild Card spot, so they'll be playing hard.
Then beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 22, the Yankees play a four-game set (with a doubleheader on 9/22) against the Tampa Bay Rays that could determine in a big way who wins the AL East Division.
After that, the Yankees close the season at home with a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles.
The Yankees have already clinched a playoff berth, so it's most important for them to have Judge in October. They'd also like him for the stretch run, though, if they can have him.
"Obviously he's a key figure of what we do," Boone said after Wednesday's game. "Hopefully we get it treated and knock it out and be a factor at some point."
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Aaron Judge's Latest Injury Scare Doesn't Bode Well for Yankees

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge leaving a game the New York Yankees needed to win is a concern. Aaron Boone may have just said it was something to monitor, but any length of time without him could have clear postseason implications.
The Yankees could be getting ahead of something, but considering the stakes and New York being within striking distance of the Tampa Bay Rays, Judge leaving so suddenly should raise some red flags about his health. Plus, it wouldn't be the first time the organization underplayed a situation to later reveal the player is more hurt than they initially let on.
If Judge returns by the weekend, the Yankees will have avoided a catastrophe. Things get tricky, though, if he's out for the rest of the season, or if he's out for a bit and then returns just in time for the playoffs.
The Yankees have faced this situation before. This happened to Edwin Encarnacion and Gary Sanchez in 2019. It happened again to Matt Carpenter in 2021.
In 2019, Encarnacion went 5-for-21, having just one hit in the ALCS, and Sanchez went 4-for-31. Carpenter was even worse. He returned in the ALCS and struck out nine times in 12 at-bats.
The Yankees can't afford to be without Judge again
Judge returning at any point is better than him being on the shelf, but without any rehab games, it's fair to wonder what he could even do — especially off postseason pitching. Sure he'll be fresher than he was in previous years, but at that point, knocking off the rust is an issue, too.
Outside of the one homer this week, he has already struggled to hit against the Colorado Rockies and Minnesota Twins starters. The Yankees aren't seeing Tomoyuki Sugano and Ryan Feltner in the postseason.
Plus, it's no secret that the Yankees with Judge and without him are a completely different team. Without their captain, the Yankees were one of the worst offenses in the sport. While he was out, their .228 batting average was the second-worst in all of baseball. Only the Seattle Mariners were worse during that span. Their .682 OPS was the fourth-worst, and their 90 wRC+ was the third-worst.
In many ways, it was reminiscent of the offense in 2023, when Judge crashed into the wall at Dodger Stadium. Their only saving grace was their rotation and bullpen. If Judge is out, pitching will have to carry them again.
It's hard to say how the Yankees would scrape together a few runs when that was already hard enough with him. They certainly made Zebby Matthews look like an ace on Wednesday, and Judge was there for the majority of his start.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Elly De La Cruz joins Lou Gehrig as only player in MLB history to accomplish remarkable feat
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz has accomplished a feat not seen in MLB in almost a century. De La Cruz became the first player since Lou Gehrig in June 1930 to hit 21 singles, 10 doubles, 8 home runs, 23 runs scored, 10 walks and steal four bases during a 23-game on-base streak. Matching a nearly 100-year-old milestone Aug 19, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz (44) fields a ground out by St. Louis Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn (0) during the sixth
item.content:encoded:
Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz has accomplished a feat not seen in MLB in almost a century.
De La Cruz became the first player since Lou Gehrig in June 1930 to hit 21 singles, 10 doubles, 8 home runs, 23 runs scored, 10 walks and steal four bases during a 23-game on-base streak.
Matching a nearly 100-year-old milestone
Aug 19, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz (44) fields a ground out by St. Louis Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn (0) during the sixth inning at Great American Ball Park. Mandatory Credit: Tanner Pearson-Imagn Images
The 24-year-old hit a two-run homer in a 6-2 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday to reach 23 straight games on-base and equal Gehrig's unique accomplishment. It was his career-best 28th home run of the season.
De La Cruz has a .286 batting average, a .364 OBP, and a .885 OPS through 133 games with the Reds this season, all of which are career-high numbers, but his future in Cincinnati is in question.
MORE: White Sox dream MLB season quickly evaporating
Contract uncertainty looms over breakout season
May 27, 2026; New York City, New York, USA; Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz (44) throws out New York Mets right fielder Brett Baty (7) (not pictured) after fielding a ground ball during the second inning at Citi Field. Mandatory Credit: Gregory Fisher-Imagn Images
De La Cruz's agent, Scott Boras, has made it known that the young shortstop is not likely to sign an early contract extension with the Reds. He reportedly turned down an offer from the Reds that would have been the largest contract in franchise history back in January, and is set to enter arbitration for the first time following the 2026 MLB season. He will be eligible for free agency in the winter of 2029.
The Reds are well out of the playoff picture as the end of the regular season approaches. They are in last place in the National League Central division, 12 games behind the Milwaukee Brewers, and will play the final game of a four-game series against the Dodgers on Thursday, where De La Cruz could extend his on-base streak to 24 games.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Elly De La Cruz Matches Lou Gehrig's Historic 23-Game On-Base Record

item.content:encoded:
Cincinnati Reds shortstop Elly De La Cruz joined New York Yankees legend Lou Gehrig in MLB history Wednesday night.
De La Cruz reached base for the 23rd consecutive game during Cincinnati's 6-2 win over the Los Angeles Dodgers. According to OptaSTATS, he matched Gehrig as the only players in the modern era to produce the same statistical combination across a 23-game stretch.
De La Cruz also launched his 28th home run of the season, helping Cincinnati secure an impressive win over the Dodgers.
Elly De La Cruz during his 23-game on-base streak:
21 singles
10 doubles
8 home runs
23 runs scored
10 walks
4 stolen bases
Only one other MLB player in the modern era has reached all of those marks over any 23-game span: Lou Gehrig (June 9-30, 1930). pic.twitter.com/sRH9xJpAhc
During his 23-game on-base streak, De La Cruz has recorded 21 singles, 10 doubles, eight home runs, 23 runs, 10 walks and four stolen bases. Gehrig produced those same totals during a 23-game stretch from June 9-30, 1930.
The 24-year-old shortstop has been one of Cincinnati's most productive players throughout the 2026 season. He is batting .286 with 150 hits, 29 doubles, five triples, 28 home runs, 74 RBIs, 94 runs and 26 stolen bases in 133 games.
De La Cruz is also approaching another milestone. With 28 home runs and 26 stolen bases, he needs only two homers and four steals over Cincinnati's final 10 games to reach 30-30 for the first time in his career.
His recent production has given the Reds another reason to look toward the future despite their position in the standings. Cincinnati entered Thursday with a 71-81 record and had already been eliminated from postseason contention.
For now, De La Cruz's historic stretch gives the Reds something to follow through the final games of the season. He will have another chance to add to both his on-base streak and his home run total as Cincinnati closes out the year.

item.content:encoded:
On Thursday, the New York Yankees are off following a three-game series with the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
They won two out of three games in the series, but most recently lost by a score of 5-4 on Wednesday afternoon.
Yankees Legend Makes Gerrit Cole Statement
While the Yankees are in the middle of a very strong 2026 season (and recently clinched a spot in the playoffs), Gerrit Cole has been struggling.
The former Cy Young Award winner has let up nine earned runs over his last two starts.
In a recent interview (via The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman), Yankees legend David Cone was asked about Cole (h/t New York Post Sports).
Heyman: “And really, what’s going on with Cole? Who’s arguably the best pitcher over the last decade?”
Cone: “Gerrit Cole, I think there’s a couple of things going on here. Post-Tommy John, obviously, it’s a mixed bag. You don’t know what to expect. I think he’s been much better than we thought he would be at this point. The problems over the last two starts are keeping the ball in the ballpark. The home runs are a problem. I think it’s down to the secondary pitches, his slider and curveball. It’s hard to be a four-pitch pitcher all the time. Sometimes you need to be a two-pitch pitcher when you’re struggling. The wheels are spinning when he does get two strikes or when he does get in a position where he needs to throw a slider or a curveball, a knuckle-curve or a changeup. He’s kind of caught in between on which pitch to use to which batter. And for me, the knuckle-curve should be to left-handed batters and the slider should be to right-handed batters. And the quality of those pitches are what protect your fastball. It’s sort of like you go to The Sopranos. You go to protection mode. You need some protection for that fastball. And his last start, there was a lot of hard contact, a lot of 100-mile-an-hour type exit velocities off of his fastball.”
Cole is in the middle of his 6th season pitching for the Yankees.
He has gone 8-9 with a 3.67 ERA in 20 starts this year.

item.title: [Friars on Base] Padres-Jazz Chisholm Jr. prediction raises a costly infield question for A.J. Preller

item.content:encoded:
With the San Diego Padres fighting for their playoff lives down the stretch, it's not necessarily the best moment in time to look ahead to the offseason. However, with the impending lockout threatening to truncate free agency and the trade market -- there's only about one month between the end of the World Series and the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement on Dec. 1 -- it's important to keep our ears to the ground regarding any noise surrounding the Friars.
And, wouldn't you know it, there's some rumors going around that the Padres could find themselves invested in one of the best hitters set to become available: Jazz Chisholm Jr. CBS' Mike Axisa attached the two parties in a free agency preview, noting that the Friars (and Rangers) are two of the best potential landing spots for the two-time All-Star.
Of course, the question isn't whether or not the Padres would actually get involved in Chisholm's market; he's been worth 11.8 fWAR over the past three seasons while hitting 74 homers and stealing 111 bases. It's merely a matter of fit, considering the long-term infield picture in San Diego.
Padres' prior investments will likely preclude them from making a serious run at Jazz Chisholm Jr. in free agency
Save for first base, which has completely been taken over by Ty France, the Padres have an expensive, aging veteran at every infield position already on the roster. Jake Cronenworth (four years, $49 million remaining on his contract after 2026), Xander Bogaerts (seven years, $178.15 million remaining), and Manny Machado (seven years, $273.63 million remaining) are all locked in for the foreseeable future.
You could push Cronenworth over to first in order to make room for an excellent second base defender like Chisholm, but is that really advisable when the Yankees' star will require another nine-figure investment? Chisholm would bring some much-needed youth to the picture -- he won't turn 29 until February -- but he'll still be in his thirties for the majority of his next contract.
For what it's worth, that prediction article also forecasts that the Padres will lose Michael King, Adrian Morejon, and Casey Mize to free agency. Thats the kind of trade-off that will have to be made given the team's finances, though I'd wager most fans would rather see an investment in the pitching staff rather than the offense. If anything, the Padres should be looking to offload some of their position-player talent in order to make room for rotation help.
With a thin talent pool and impending lockout speeding up the urgency of the offseason calendar, this is the kind of decision that A.J. Preller and company will have to make before we get to free agency. There won't be many players of Chisholm's ilk available this winter, but passing on him for the sake of a more cohesive roster is probably for the best.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler, Rays' Junior Caminero Are Crashing Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Party
Welcome to MLB's potentially permanent post-Aaron Judge MVP landscape. Now it's a three-horse AL MVP race, still undecided even in the last 10 days of the season.
It's Yordan Alvarez vs. Junior Caminero vs. Cam Schlittler. Choose your fighter.
If there is a favorite, it's Alvarez. He's had one hand on the AL MVP for most of the season, and FanDuel is ready to assume he'll eventually get the other hand on it. Here are their current odds:
TOP NEWS
Brutal Mets x Alonso Stat 🤢
Every Team's Biggest Offseason Decision 🧐
Yanks Could Be LOADED Next Year 😤
- Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros: -20000
- Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays: +1400
- Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees: +7000
- Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals: +10000
However, the tide is turning. Yankees manager Aaron Boone is openly pondering whether Schlittler deserves the MVP. And after hitting two walk-off home runs in four games, Caminero has turned a low hum of an MVP case into a loud scream.
Is this an erasure of what Alvarez has done? Or are there genuine cases for Caminero and Schlittler? Let's discuss.
Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Case Is Ironclad… Sort Of
The Gist: He leads the AL in everything, but his case does break down upon examination.
Alvarez came into 2026 with a conundrum. He was clearly one of baseball's best hitters, yet he had never led the AL in any key statistical category.
Talk about making up for lost time. The 29-year-old has stayed healthy and mashed all year, resulting in AL-leading marks in:
- AVG: .310
- OBP: .428
- SLG: .594
- OPS: 1.022
- OPS+: 188
Alvarez also has 39 home runs and 98 RBI, putting him just two and four off the AL-leading paces set by Caminero and Pete Alonso. We're still on Triple Crown watch with Alvarez.
There's just one problem: Alvarez has gone kind of cold.
That is, "cold" relative to his own standards. Through the end of July, Alvarez had a 1.077 OPS and 35 homers. Since August 1, he has a .860 OPS with four homers. Nick Sogard has more homers since then, and he began his major league career with 252 plate appearances without going deep even once.
If this year's MVP voters want to hold the AL West against Alvarez, that wouldn't be unfair. It's a historically bad division, and Alvarez has benefited to the tune of an MLB-high 447 plate appearances against teams with losing records through play on Tuesday.
He has a 1.118 OPS against those teams, compared to a .817 OPS against all others. That's an unflattering 301-point gap.
Junior Caminero Has the Vibes
The Gist: There's more here than just the home runs.
Caminero's 41 homers are the only true statistical advantage he has over Alvarez. Unless, of course, you want to count double plays grounded into. For the second year in a row, Caminero leads in that category, too.
Aside from that, Alvarez has a 1.024 OPS vs. Caminero's .897 OPS. It's also Alvarez's 6.1 rWAR vs. Caminero's 5.6 rWAR.
So what does Caminero's AL MVP case come down to? Vibes, mostly.
There's only a minuscule difference between Caminero's performance against losing teams (.908 OPS) and winning teams (.880 OPS). That has mattered to a Rays squad that built its AL-best 92-59 record in part by going 38-24 against other winning teams.
This is a form of clutchness in itself, and some argue it matters more than Alvarez's generic blend of clutchness. Even there, the comparison between the two is basically Great vs. Greater. In high-leverage spots, for example, Caminero has a .958 OPS to Alvarez's 1.190 OPS. Nothing wrong with either one.
The other side of the ball matters, too. Caminero hasn't started even one game at designated hitter, compared to 126 for Alvarez. While Caminero hardly has a sterling reputation at third base, Mike Petriello of MLB.com noted that he has moved into positive territory in Fielding Run Value since the start of June.
Cam Schlittler Is More Than an Also-Ran
The Gist: According to one stat, he should be the favorite.
Aaron Judge? He knows a thing or three about MVP awards. So what does he think about the Yankees' right-handed ace winning it this year?
"They've got a Cy Young Award for a reason—best pitcher in the game," Judge said, per Chris Kirschner of The Athletic. "He's got my vote, definitely, for the Cy Young."
Harsh… but fair? Not if you look at Schlittler's ranks on the AL leaderboard! He's the leader in:
- ERA: 1.95
- ERA+: 216
- WHIP: 0.904
- WAR: 7.0
Those first three are impressive marks for a pitcher. That last one is impressive, period. By rWAR, Schlittler literally is the most valuable player in the AL.
This isn't necessarily an automatic mic drop for MVP voters. As Brian Murphy of MLB.com noted, eight full-time pitchers have led the AL in rWAR over the last 30 years, and only one (Justin Verlander in 2011) won the MVP.
Context matters, though. In this case, Schlittler has been a constant in a season otherwise marked by turmoil for the Yankees. He's allowed two earned runs or fewer in 25 of his 31 starts, making him the only pitcher who can claim that. The Yankees are 19-6 in those games.
Predicting Who Comes Out on Top
The Gist: It could be close.
Here's the thing about Alvarez as the heavy AL MVP favorite: He's the favorite because he should be.
We talked about the numbers. What we didn't talk about is how screwed the Astros would be without him. For example, they are 20-14 in games where he's hit at least one home run. Eliminate or greatly reduce those 34 games, and they're not hanging onto the AL West lead with a 76-76 record.
It should also work in Alvarez's favor that there isn't a united front behind Caminero or Schlittler. They could end up merely splitting whatever votes don't go to Alvarez. And if any of the three is going to get more than one-third of the bunch, it's probably Alvarez.
Even so, it's hard to ignore the feeling that Alvarez's case is more precarious than it should be.
Whereas his MVP creds peaked in July and have been in stasis ever since, Caminero and Schlittler have been busy strengthening theirs. They also play on better teams in a better division that tends to have more eyes on it. I'm told they call it "East Coast bias."
Nobody likes boring predictions, so here goes with a bold call for how the AL MVP voting will play out:
- Junior Caminero
- Yordan Alvarez
- Cam Schlittler
I'm caught between thinking Caminero shouldn't win it and thinking he shouldn't not win it. What's clear is that he wants the AL MVP and is pushing hard for it. Those two walk-offs are just two of four homers he's hit in his last 10 games. It doesn't make for a bad narrative that it's service of a Rays team that is outpacing a Yankees team that is spending three times as much money on payroll.
So, congratulations to Junior Caminero. Or, sorry for the jinx. It depends on what actually happens.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] La última Salida De Carlos Rodón Supone Un Nuevo Motivo De Preocupación Para Los Yankees En El Peor Momento Posible

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Carlos Rodón lanzó seis entradas para los Yankees el miércoles y evitó que se les escapara una tarde complicada, pero las estadísticas finales no lo dicen todo. El zurdo cedió dos carreras y cuatro hits, concedió tres bases por bolas y ponchó a cinco en 102 lanzamientos , en la derrota por 5-4 de Nueva York, en la 13.ª entrada, ante los Minnesota Twins en el Target Field.
Rodón se fue del partido con los Yankees perdiendo por 2-0. Anthony Volpe igualó el marcador con un doble de dos carreras en la novena entrada, y Nueva York se puso por delante tanto en la décima como en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que un sencillo de Víctor Caratini, como bateador suplente, puso fin al partido en la decimotercera entrada. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, mientras que John Schreiber se llevó la derrota.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 88-64. Tampa Bay ganó más tarde ese mismo miércoles, lo que deja a Nueva York a 4,5 partidos de los Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero las decisiones que tengan que tomar ahora sobre la rotación de lanzadores tendrán repercusiones en la clasificación de la división y en el orden de salida en octubre.
Los resultados de Rodón siguen siendo sólidos. El miércoles sumó su 25.ª salida consecutiva en la que ha cedido tres carreras limpias o menos, todo un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees. Además, ha encadenado dos salidas de calidad seguidas y ha logrado su quinta salida de calidad en 15 partidos, después de haber lanzado 6 1/3 entradas contra los Mets en su anterior salida.
Su carga de trabajo también ha ido por buen camino. Rodon lanzó 102 lanzamientos el miércoles, su mejor marca de la temporada, tras haber llegado a los 93 lanzamientos contra los Mets. Desde que volvió de la lista de lesionados a mediados de agosto, tiene una efectividad de 2,40, un WHIP de 0,93 y una relación de 31 ponches por cada 12 bases por bolas en 30 entradas.
Para los Yankees, sin embargo, la pregunta que surge tras la visita a Minnesota no es si Rodon podrá aguantar una salida. Es si podrá recuperar su potencia habitual lo suficientemente rápido, ahora que las alineaciones de octubre dejan menos margen para una puesta en marcha gradual.
El calendario deja a los Yankees poco tiempo para distinguir entre una fluctuación temporal y una tendencia que se repita.
Los primeros 55 lanzamientos cuentan una historia diferente
La preocupación se notó desde el principio en todo el repertorio de lanzamientos de Rodon, no solo en su bola rápida de cuatro costuras. La instantánea del seguimiento de lanzamientos adjunta a la salida mostraba que sus cinco lanzamientos estaban por debajo de su velocidad media de la temporada tras 55 lanzamientos.
Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,6 mph, frente a la media de la temporada de 94,4 mph, lo que supone una caída de 1,8 mph. Su slider bajó 1,4 mph, su cambio de velocidad 2,3 mph, su sinker 1,9 mph y su curva 1,1 mph.
Recurrió a la bola rápida de cuatro costuras en el 45 % de esos primeros 55 lanzamientos y al slider en el 29 %. Eso significa que casi tres cuartas partes de su repertorio inicial procedían de dos lanzamientos que estaban 1,8 mph y 1,4 mph por debajo de sus valores habituales de la temporada.
Eso hace que esa caída inicial sea más notable que el dato de una sola bola rápida. El cambio de velocidad fue el que mostró la mayor diferencia, mientras que ambos tipos de bola rápida estaban casi 2 mph por debajo de sus niveles anuales.
Pero Rodon no se quedó ahí. Su bola rápida de cuatro costuras alcanzó una media de 92,3 mph en la primera entrada, 92,8 en la segunda y 92,4 en la tercera. En la cuarta, esa media subió a 94,9 mph, y más tarde lanzó varios lanzamientos por encima de las 95 mph.
Rodon necesitaba tiempo para soltarse un poco
Rodon habló después sobre su mal comienzo. La información disponible tras el partido no especificaba que esa rigidez se debiera a su codo. Describió cómo se sentía al principio, antes de que su velocidad mejorara a medida que avanzaba el partido.
Rodon dijo que empezó el partido un poco «tenso» antes de soltarse.
Esa formulación es importante por su historial médico de 2026. Rodon empezó la temporada en la lista de lesionados tras someterse a una operación durante la pretemporada para extirparle un espolón óseo del codo izquierdo. Más tarde volvió a la lista de lesionados por una inflamación en el codo izquierdo y se reincorporó el 18 de agosto tras un periodo de rehabilitación.
No se determinó que esa molestia fuera un problema en el codo, y no se informó de ninguna nueva lesión de Rodon tras el partido. Aun así, los Yankees tendrán motivos para estar atentos a la rapidez con la que recupere su velocidad en su próxima salida, tras una temporada acortada por las lesiones.
Los buenos resultados están ocultando una carga de trabajo más intensa
La eficacia de Rodón se ha mantenido intacta, aunque la forma de llegar a las seis entradas haya cambiado. Contra los Mets, el 11 de septiembre, necesitó 93 lanzamientos para completar 6 1/3 entradas, concedió una base por bolas y ponchó a ocho. Cinco días después, necesitó 102 lanzamientos para completar seis entradas, con tres bases por bolas y cinco ponches.
De los 102 lanzamientos del miércoles, solo 59 fueron strikes, algo menos del 58 %. Aun así, limitó a Minnesota a cuatro hits y dos carreras, pero el mayor número de corredores en base y los conteos más ajustados hicieron que esta salida le costara más esfuerzo que su anterior salida.
Teniendo en cuenta sus estadísticas de la temporada hasta el miércoles y su actuación final contra Minnesota, Rodon tiene ahora una ERA de aproximadamente 2,95 en 76 1/3 entradas repartidas en 15 salidas como titular. Los Yankees han contado con él para evitar que el rival anote cuando ha estado disponible.
La salida de los Rays sube el listón
Se espera que la próxima salida de Rodón sea durante la serie de cuatro partidos en casa de los Yankeescontra Tampa Bay, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada dividida en el Yankee Stadium. Nueva York lleva un balance de 3-6 contra los Rays esta temporada.
Ese partido podría ser su última salida como titular en la temporada regular. Además, les da a los Yankees la oportunidad de comprobar directamente si la caída en la velocidad de los lanzamientos del miércoles fue algo puntual o algo que le va a acompañar a Rodon en la postemporada.
Los Yankees obtendrán su siguiente dato cuando le toque lanzar a Rodon contra Tampa Bay, con la lucha por el título de división y la rotación de la postemporada aún en juego.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees’ Clarke Schmidt flashes solid stuff in ‘emotional’ return from Tommy John surgery
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: MINNESOTA — Fresh off the injured list in time for a morning report to the visitor’s clubhouse at Target Field, Clarke Schmidt searched for a pick-me-up on Wednesday. item.content:encoded:
MINNESOTA — Fresh off the injured list in time for a morning report to the visitor’s clubhouse at Target Field, Clarke Schmidt searched for a pick-me-up on Wednesday.
The Yankees’ pitcher, eagerly anticipating his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery, wanted nothing more than to take the mound later in the day. But first, he craved a cup of coffee. A latte, preferably.
And if he couldn’t find one?
“Day over,” Schmidt joked. “Not activated.”
It turns out that Schmidt didn’t really need the caffeine, as he was plenty amped up by the time he was summed into the Yankees’ 13-inning, 5-4 loss to the Twins. The first man out of the bullpen — the starter is working as a reliever since he didn’t have time to build up — Schmidt took over for Carlos Rodón with the Bombers down 2-0 in the seventh inning.
It was his first appearance since July 3, 2025.
“It’s a lot like your debut,” Schmidt said. “Thankfully, I’m a little bit more comfortable now, but I think it was similar emotions and a surge of adrenaline.”
Schmidt added that entering the game was “emotional,” and that he had to focus on staying present and slowing things down as he exited the bullpen.
“He looked pretty sharp and didn’t look sped up or overwhelmed at all,” Aaron Boone said. “It’s a tight ballgame there, your first game in over a year, and I’m sure there’s some emotions there. I thought he handled all that pretty well. Hopefully, as he goes now, he’ll get a little sharper.”
That’s not to say that Schmidt didn’t flash potential with the Yankees hoping he can factor into their postseason bullpen. He and Boone were happy with the right-hander’s stuff, and the fact that Schmidt got two swinging strikeouts.
His velocity, meanwhile, topped out at 95.8 mph over 24 pitches.
But Schmidt only got two outs and had to be relieved by Brent Headrick, who got out of the inning unscathed, after allowing two singles. Each knock came on weak contact, but Boone also felt Schmidt’s execution on those pitches could have been better.
Schmidt, meanwhile, was frustrated that he got into three three-ball counts over four batters faced.
Still, the 30-year-old was happy to be an active pitcher again, even if that meant prematurely warming up during a rocky first inning for Rodón.
“In traditional bullpen fashion, I got dry humped a little bit in the first,” Schmidt said with a laugh. “I thought Carlos was coming out, and I was excited and the adrenaline was at a high. And then I had to sit back down and settle down for a second.”
Before and after Wednesday’s game, Schmidt took time to reflect on his long road back from his second Tommy John operation, which he called “not an easy journey at all.” The hardest part, he said, was spending so much time away from the game and a lot of “long, monotonous days” of rehab.
“It was almost like a zero dark thirty-type feel. It’s like you rinse, wash, repeat. You’re doing the same thing every single day,” Schmidt said. “It’s trying to get as much sleep as you can, showing up early in the morning and before the team’s there, and putting all the work in and then staying for the game.
“You learn a lot about yourself spiritually and how to continue to just keep going and keep being resilient.”
Schmidt noted that he leaned on his faith and family a lot to get through the grueling rehab process, so he appreciated that his father, Dwight, a pilot for Delta Air Lines, was able to rearrange his work schedule and make it to Minnesota on Wednesday.
“He’s a trooper, man,” Schmidt said. “[My family] always tries to have one family member at my outings. I’ve been so blessed and so lucky to have a family who’s supportive of me and has been with me every step of the way. I know I wouldn’t be where I’m at without them.”

item.title: [heavy.com] Reds' Elly De La Cruz Makes Baseball History Only Done by Lou Gehrig
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: There are certain names that pop up that emphasize a particular feat on a baseball diamond as remarkably impressive. Lou Gehrig is one of those names, and that’s the company that Cincinnati Reds superstar Elly De La Cruz is keeping lately. De La Cruz just did something so rare that it hasn’t been accomplished in Major League Baseball since Gehrig did it for the New York Yankees nearly 100 years ago. The game has obviously changed a lot, but the idea that the statistics of this sport tie it back
item.content:encoded:
There are certain names that pop up that emphasize a particular feat on a baseball diamond as remarkably impressive.
Lou Gehrig is one of those names, and that’s the company that Cincinnati Reds superstar Elly De La Cruz is keeping lately.
De La Cruz just did something so rare that it hasn’t been accomplished in Major League Baseball since Gehrig did it for the New York Yankees nearly 100 years ago.
The game has obviously changed a lot, but the idea that the statistics of this sport tie it back into eras so long in the past is a remarkable feature of baseball.
And it really emphasizes just how remarkable De La Cruz has been down the stretch of this season.
Elly De La Cruz Makes Baseball History
De La Cruz is currently on a 23-game on-base streak, which is impressive but not the history he made.
The history comes from his exact statistical combination during the 23-game streak, which was shared by OptaStats.
In the 23 games, De La Cruz has:
- 21 singles
- 10 doubles
- 8 home runs
- 23 runs scored
- 10 walks
- 4 stolen bases
It’s a combination of six stats that has not been matched in a 23-game stretch in MLB history since Gehrig.
OptaStats writes that Gehrig did it in June 1930. That’s 96 years ago.
Elly De La Cruz during his 23-game on-base streak:
21 singles
10 doubles
8 home runs
23 runs scored
10 walks
4 stolen bases
Only one other MLB player in the modern era has reached all of those marks over any 23-game span: Lou Gehrig (June 9-30, 1930). pic.twitter.com/sRH9xJpAhc
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) September 17, 2026
Interestingly enough, that 1930 season was one of the rare years back then that the Yankees didn’t even reach the World Series. And in those days, either you won the American League pennant or you missed the playoffs entirely — there were no earlier rounds.
So despite Gehrig’s incredible feat, the Yankees missed the playoffs in 1930. And the Reds are comfortably missing the playoffs in 2026.
Of course, that’s not the part of the parallel anyone in Cincinnati wants to focus on. It’s worth simply appreciating how good De La Cruz has been.
Elly’s Future
The question that will begin to be more and more on the minds in Cincinnati is that of the future of De La Cruz.
His agent Scott Boras is already making noise about the fact that down the road, he doesn’t think De La Cruz will sign an early contract extension with the Reds.
That puts pressure on the Reds to ensure their roster is competitive sooner rather than later — both to impress Elly but also to make the most of the time they still have with him.
In various ways, De La Cruz is a historically special baseball player. At least for a few more years it seems, he’ll be doing that in a Reds uniform.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Anthony Volpe's position switch looks like something Yankees should've done a long time ago
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe is four games into his new role as a big-league second baseman after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Volpe hasn't committed an error yet, and while the sample is tiny, the eye test feels so right. Volpe just looks comfortable out there. His Jeter-esque jump throw on Sunday (from second base, but still!) was such a rewarding watch for Yankees fans who have experienced the dreadful lows of Volpe's up-and-down season
item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe is four games into his new role as a big-league second baseman after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list with a sprained right thumb. Volpe hasn't committed an error yet, and while the sample is tiny, the eye test feels so right. Volpe just looks comfortable out there.
His Jeter-esque jump throw on Sunday (from second base, but still!) was such a rewarding watch for Yankees fans who have experienced the dreadful lows of Volpe's up-and-down season and career. It looked and felt so much more iconic than it was.
It didn't take long for Anthony Volpe to learn second base for the Yankees
Volpe looking smooth at second is a bittersweet reality for Yankees fans, especially those with a quick trigger to criticize the team's development and roster decisions. On one hand, New York's decision to send Volpe down to the minors and learn second base this season has ... worked! On the other hand, this exact plan should have been put into motion a long time ago.
It's kind of like turning in your book report a month late in middle school. The teacher is like, "Well, thanks ... but I just remembered again that you never handed this in." You might've been better off just taking the zero and acing the next one.
If Volpe keeps acing second base — and sustains this level of defense into 2027 and beyond alongside George Lombard Jr. — the Yankees will have salvaged Volpe's career and somewhat made up for their entire mishandling of his development.
Then again, should the Yankees really get any credit for salvaging anything here, especially since it was the organization itself that contributed to this mess? Even now, it took an injury to Chisholm (not his horrid season and Volpe's red-hot bat in the minors) to give Volpe another opportunity. This decision was made for the Yankees, not by them. And it came way, way too late. On second thought, they don't get any credit here.
Anthony Volpe as a second-base solution should have been obvious to the Yankees years ago
Any player evaluator of worth should have been able to look at Volpe and surmise that a move from shortstop to second base made sense. Volpe won a Gold Glove as a rookie shortstop in 2023, but his range, arm, and consistency declined after that. Isn't that pretty much the precise recipe for a move from short to second, if you had to literally write the script?
The Yankees' problem with Volpe over the years, as has been acknowledged ad nauseam, is that they made "New York Yankees starting shortstop" Volpe's identity (rather than his job) and hugged that identity too tightly. It became a stranglehold that suffocated Volpe and had Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman at their most delusional in interviews, which is saying a lot.
The funny thing is that Volpe's never been against changing positions. He said unironically that he'd play catcher. It was Boone and Cashman who were stubborn, and they never actually lessened their grip on this situation. George Lombard Jr. undid that grip for them, and then Chisholm went down.
To the non-Yankee fan, the Yankees might look smart for putting Volpe at second base. But for the die-hards, this decision — and Volpe's good performance at second so far — hurts as much as it excites. At least for now.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Yankees, Cardinals Intriguing Trade Idea Involving Anthony Volpe
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Razo
item.description: The New York Yankees are focused on the postseason and are looking to end their World Series drought, which has lasted over 15 years. Nonetheless, there are takes and opinions to help the team improve this upcoming offseason. It's been a rollercoaster 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old's best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere. Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are focused on the postseason and are looking to end their World Series drought, which has lasted over 15 years. Nonetheless, there are takes and opinions to help the team improve this upcoming offseason.
It's been a rollercoaster 2026 MLB season for Anthony Volpe, who was optioned to Triple-A in August and then recalled in September. Still, it might be in the 25-year-old's best interest to get a fresh start elsewhere.
Christopher Kline of FanSided floated a trade idea that would send Volpe along with LHP Brent Headrick and LHP Kyle Carr to the St. Louis Cardinals for 24-year-old shortstop Masyn Winn.
"The Yankees' lack of fundamental soundness on the defensive end has bitten them in the you-know-what all season, just like it did last year," Kline wrote in a Sept. 16 article. "The hope was that top prospect George Lombard Jr. could steady the ship at shortstop, but he has stacked up errors left and right.
"It's too early to write off the 21-year-old long term, but he could serve more comfortably at third or second — which is notable, since Jazz Chisholm Jr. is about to [be a free agent]. Winn immediately alleviates a ton of defensive issues for the Yankees, while his weaker bat would be well-protected in the American League's most potent lineup."
Yankees Have Assets to Trade for Cardinals' Masyn Winn
Since being recalled on Sept. 9, Volpe has performed well. Entering Sept. 17, Volpe has been batting .348 with eight hits, a home run, seven RBIs, and three runs scored in seven games, per StatMuse. Meanwhile, Kline believes Volpe can benefit from a move, while the Yankees would upgrade their defense in the infield with Winn.
"New York has the resources to one day pay Winn his worth, too, although three additional years of club control means those conversations are in the distant future," Kline added in his article. "This move allows St. Louis to bump Wetherholt to shortstop and plug in former top prospect Anthony Volpe at second base, where he has looked much more solid of late in New York."
Anthony Volpe Would Benefit From a Move Out of New York
As for what Winn can bring to the plate, entering Sept. 17, he has a batting average of .237 with 107 hits, five homers, 54 RBIs, and 52 runs scored in 129 games this season, per StatMuse.
Moreover, Volpe would benefit from a move to the Cardinals, where Kline believes the team could move him to second base, where he might thrive. The two bullpen arms would bolster St. Louis' bullpen and still have a handful of years under control to help in their rebuild.
"Volpe is a former Gold Glove shortstop whose defensive profile is very much salvageable, especially at a less demanding position," Kline noted in his article. "He's also a hitter with more upside right now, with the potential to add real pop to the back half of St. Louis' lineup.
"The Cardinals also add high-leverage reliever Brent Headrick, with a 1.94 ERA and five years of club control, and 24-year-old southpaw Kyle Carr, a Triple-A arm who profiles as a potential back-end starter with plus command."
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.

The post Yankees, Cardinals Intriguing Trade Idea Involving Anthony Volpe appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] “We Can’t Have This,” “Another Bust” – Fans Rip Spencer Jones After 5-Strikeout Nightmare Puts Him in Unwanted Aaron Judge Territory
item.dc:creator: Karan Tyagi
item.description: While it has been a fairly decent year for New York Yankees rookie OF Spencer Jones, an uncharacteristic performance in Wednesday's series finale against the Minnesota Twins at Target Field has put the 25-year-old under the scanner, with multiple fans sharing their concerns and criticizing him on social media. Jones went 0-for-6 in the series finale, striking out five times, and became the first Yankee to post that record since captain Aaron Judge did so during his slump in 2024. Jones struggled
item.content:encoded:
While it has been a fairly decent year for New York Yankees rookie OF Spencer Jones, an uncharacteristic performance in Wednesday's series finale against the Minnesota Twins at Target Field has put the 25-year-old under the scanner, with multiple fans sharing their concerns and criticizing him on social media.
Jones went 0-for-6 in the series finale, striking out five times, and became the first Yankee to post that record since captain Aaron Judge did so during his slump in 2024. Jones struggled at the plate, prompting multiple fan reactions to his performance.
Here are some fan reactions to Jones' five-strikeout night:
"We can't have this October is around the corner," one fan commented.
"Another bust lol," another fan commented.
The Yankees lost 5-4 in extra innings, missing the chance to secure the sweep in Minnesota. The Bombers fell further in the race for the AL East crown and are now 4.5 games behind the divisional leaders, the Tampa Bay Rays.
Spencer Jones Also Had a Couple of Errors During the Twins Series
On Wednesday night, Jones failed to catch a simple fly ball to center field, allowing Kody Clemens to reach second base. Carlos Rodon showed no visible reaction to the play.
Earlier in the series opener on Monday night, Jones committed a defensive error in left-center field when the ball dipped under his glove, allowing the Twins to score two runs at the plate and prompting a frustrated reaction from starting pitcher Will Warren.
While it might have been a topsy-turvy series for the rookie outfielder, he has ensured that he is worthy of being on the active roster as October baseball nears, with 10 games left in the regular season.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Lombard Se Lleva La Culpa, Pero La Derrota Por 5-4 De Los Yankees Ante Los Twins, Tras 13 Entradas, Tiene Muchos Culpables
item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Anthony Volpe bateó con tanta fuerza que perdió el equilibrio, convencido de que la pelota se había ido fuera. En cambio, rebotó contra el muro alto del centro-derecha, un doble de dos carreras que igualó el marcador para los Yankees con dos outs en la novena entrada. Durante un momento intenso y emocionante el miércoles, Nueva York parecía dispuesta a llevarse la barrida.
Lo que vino después fueron cuatro entradas más en las que el equipo llegaba hasta la puerta y se negaba a cruzarla. Los Yankees se pusieron por delante en la décima. Volvieron a hacerlo en la undécima. Llenaron las bases sin outs en la duodécima. Cada vez acababan con un empate o con una remontada desperdiciada.
Un viaje que debería haber acabado con una barrida acabó poniendo de manifiesto el único punto débil que un aspirante al título no puede permitirse arrastrar hasta octubre. No se trató de un colapso del bullpen ni de un rebote desafortunado. Fue la alineación de los Yankees la que no paraba de preparar la mesa, pero nunca se sentaba a comer.
La culpa final recayó en un novato que no se la merecía él solo.
Los Minnesota Twins vencieron a los Yankees por 5-4 en 13 entradas, poniendo fin a ese partido maratoniano con un sencillo de Victor Caratini en la primera base que rebotó en el montículo y se coló por debajo del guante de George Lombard Jr. en la segunda base. Con esta derrota, Nueva York queda con un balance de 88-64, a cuatro partidos de los Rays de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, a falta de 10 partidos por disputar. Los Yankees ya tienen asegurada su plaza en los playoffs, pero el título de la división y la exención de la primera ronda se les están escapando.
Una remontada que no llevó a ninguna parte
Nueva York había sumado cuatro hits en ocho entradas y perdía por 2-0, mientras que el lanzador diestro de los Twins, Zebby Matthews, había ponchado a ocho. Entonces llegó la novena entrada. Lombard conectó un sencillo, Paul Goldschmidt le siguió y el corredor suplente José Caballero preparó el terreno para Volpe.
Volpe impulsó las dos carreras, lo que le supuso al cerrador de los Twins, Yoendrys Gómez, su primer salvamento fallido del año y obligó a jugar entradas extras.
Ali Sánchez impulsó al corredor automático con un sencillo en la décima entrada, dando a los Yankees su primera ventaja. Luke Keaschall respondió con un sencillo que empató el partido ante David Bednar. Un fly de sacrificio de Caballero puso a Nueva York por delante en la undécima. Royce Lewis igualó el marcador. Dos ventajas, dos respuestas inmediatas.
La entrada que dará que hablar
La 12.ª es la entrada que los aficionados volverán a ver una y otra vez. Los Yankees llenaron las bases sin outs, la situación que debería haber sentenciado el partido. Pero no sacaron nada de ella.
Heliot Ramos, que bateaba en el turno de Aaron Judge, mandó una bola corta hacia el montículo. Travis Adams la convirtió en una doble jugada 1-2-3. Sánchez se fue con un strikeout, dejando a otros dos en base. Los Yankees acabaron con 7 de 30 con corredores en posición de anotar.
El juez se marcha y el ataque se queda con pocos jugadores
Judge se retiró en la sexta entrada por una contractura en la parte inferior de la pierna derecha que empezó a notar en la primera entrada. Falló dos veces y no volvió al campo, solo siete partidos después de una ausencia de 99 días. Por eso Ramos estaba bateando en su lugar.
El entrenador Aaron Boone describió la noche como una oportunidad perdida, no como un partido robado, y sus palabras reflejaban la importancia del momento en el calendario.
«Obviamente, muchas cosas buenas, pero no las suficientes», dijo Boone. «Ha sido un golpe duro, claro, cuando tenías la oportunidad de barrer la serie y justo antes de un día de descanso. Pero tenemos que superarlo y prepararnos para enfrentarnos a un buen equipo de los Diamondbacks».
Al final del partido, Boone no se anduvo con rodeos con Lombard, pero tampoco lo machacó.
Boone reconoció que la bola de Caratini rebotó en el montículo, pero fue una jugada que Lombard «se espera que haga y sabemos que es capaz de hacer».
Rodón lo da todo en octubre, pero no saca nada a cambio
Carlos Rodón le dio a los Yankees el comienzo que necesita una rotación en la postemporada y vio cómo se esfumaba. El zurdo encajó dos carreras en seis entradas, ampliando su récord de la franquicia a 25 salidas consecutivas en las que ha encajado tres carreras o menos. Lanzó 102 lanzamientos, su máximo de la temporada, y bajó su promedio de carreras limpias a 2,95.
«Empecé un poco lento, un poco tenso», dijo Rodon. «Me fui soltando en las siguientes entradas, así que eso estuvo bien».
Clarke Schmidt hizo su tan esperado regreso en la séptima entrada, ponchando a dos antes de que Brent Headrick dejara a dos en base. El bullpen corrió una maratón que la alineación nunca supo recompensar.
Una primicia para el club que no se veía desde 1991
Este es el dato que pocos destacarán. Ha sido la primera derrota de los Yankees tras ir ganando varias veces en entradas extras desde el 5 de mayo de 1991, en Seattle, es decir, en un lapso de más de 34 años. También fue su octava derrota en la última entrada de la temporada, un récord de la franquicia, y ningún equipo de la MLB ha encajado más hits decisivos en la última entrada en 2026, según datos de Baseball Reference. Ningún equipo de los Yankees ha perdido nunca más partidos a domicilio en entradas extras en una sola temporada.
Lo curioso es que los equipos malos no acumulan cifras como estas. Un equipo mediocre pierde en nueve partidos. Solo un buen equipo es capaz de forzar una prórroga fuera de casa una y otra vez, y luego seguir perdiéndola.
Cómo queda la carrera por la División Este de la Liga Americana
Spencer Jones lanzó su propia advertencia, ponchándose cinco veces en una noche en la que se fue de 0 de 6, lo que demostró lo rápido que se castigan los swings fallidos cuando los márgenes se estrechan. En septiembre se lee de otra manera que en julio.
Los Yankees tienen el jueves libre antes de empezar una serie de fin de semana en Arizona, donde Gerrit Cole será el lanzador titular el viernes a las 21:40 h (hora del Este). No se espera que Judge tenga que hacerse más pruebas. Nueva York ha perdido terreno que quizá no recupere y le ha dado un respiro a los Rays.
Los Yankees saben cómo ganar los partidos intermedios. Una noche en la que solo tenían que ganar uno, no pudieron.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Heliot Ramos Is Flying Under the Radar Down the Stretch for Yankees

item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge made his long-awaited return from the injured list last week, the New York Yankees subsequently reduced the playing time of fellow outfielder Heliot Ramos.
This was always the plan, as the Yankees acquired Ramos at the trade deadline to be a platoon bat against left-handed pitching. The 27-year-old's miserable start to his Bronx tenure as a starting outfielder not only cemented his bench role but also quickly made fans believe that trading for him was a huge mistake.
However, Ramos is sneakily turning things around since going to the bench, which is good, as Judge exited Wednesday's game with right lower-leg tightness. He's taking full advantage of the more sporadic at-bats he gets, driving the ball with authority and seeing results.
Heliot Ramos is figuring things out at the plate
It is worth mentioning that the game that got Ramos going came before Judge returned to the lineup and pushed him to the bench. On August 30 against the Boston Red Sox, the righty-swinging outfielder reached base in all four of his plate appearances and hit his first home run as a Yankee, a three-run shot that broke the game open.
Even then, Ramos failed to reach base in his next two games before going 1-for-2 with a single and a walk against the San Diego Padres on September 5, the last game he played before Judge was activated. But on September 8, Ramos pinch-hit for Judge in the eighth inning against the Colorado Rockies and promptly hit another three-run homer to seal another Yankee victory.
Ramos has since started two games in right field to give Judge a breather: those coming on September 12 against the New York Mets and on Tuesday night against the Minnesota Twins. Far more noteworthy was the Twins game, which saw Judge get the day off entirely.
Ramos was a key component to New York's production by going 2-for-4 with a walk, an RBI, and two runs scored; his third-inning walk allowed him to eventually score a two-out run, and he lashed an RBI double in the sixth inning that also set up a game-breaking homer by Spencer Jones shortly afterwards.
Dating back to Ramos' big day against Boston, he is slashing .350/.458/.700 in 24 plate appearances with a pair of homers, seven RBI and a 221 wRC+. Since Judge returned, Ramos has made only 11 plate appearances, but collected four hits (two for extra bases) and a walk with four RBI and three runs scored.
Even when Ramos was stuck in his terrible slump that lasted for most of August, most of the balls he put in play were hit very hard. 55.3% of Ramos' batted balls had an exit velocity of 95 mph or higher despite his miserable .119 batting average from August 4 to August 29. Ramos continues to make hard contact during his recent hot streak, with a 57.1% hard-hit rate, and the expected stats are not much lower than the actual stats (.473 xwOBA against a .488 wOBA).
Of course, the sample size is very small, and Ramos hasn't been productive in every single plate appearance. But it's still very encouraging to see him find results and come through with timely hits. As a bench player, the Yankees may rely on him even more to come through in clutch situations down the stretch, and they'd feel more comfortable putting the bat in Ramos' hands if he continues to hit.
*stats updated before Wednesday's game against the Twins
Joe Najarian is the Deputy Editor and a writer for the New York Yankees and New York Mets On SI sites. He got his bachelor’s degree in journalism with a specialization in sports from Rutgers University, graduating in 2022. Joe has previously written for Jersey Sporting News and for the New York Giants On SI site. You can follow him on Twitter/X: @JoeNajarian
Follow joenajarian

item.title: [nytimes.com] The MLB prospects I was wrong about: Jacob Misiorowski, Ben Rice and more

item.content:encoded:
At the end of every season, I look at players who’ve succeeded in the major leagues beyond the expectations I had for them, and explain where my projections went wrong. Sometimes it’s what I saw (or didn’t see); sometimes it’s a matter of incomplete information from sources, but regardless of the reasons, they’re my mistakes, and it’s on me to learn from them to improve my projections for other players who might show similarities to these players in the future.
Advertisement
I do have some general criteria for this list, as I look for players who have become regulars, either as everyday position players or bona fide starting pitchers, where I thought they’d be bench players, relievers or something less. In most cases, I look for more than one year of sustained performance at this higher level. These aren’t the only players I got wrong, for sure, but I’ve covered some in previous editions of this article (here’s last year’s and 2024’s), and I’d also rather go a little deeper on guys I got more wrong or where I can tell a clear story of why I got them wrong.
Regardless, here are a few new players where I was way too low on my projections for their major-league careers.
Jacob Misiorowski, RHP, Milwaukee Brewers
I know I wasn’t alone in my belief that Misiorowski wouldn’t hold up as a starter, either because he wouldn’t throw enough strikes or because he would break down. No one has ever thrown this hard, this much, without getting hurt. Jordan Hicks couldn’t do it. Aroldis Chapman couldn’t do it. Hunter Greene just underwent Tommy John surgery for the second time. Ben Joyce can’t even hold up in relief.
The Brewers took Misiorowski in the second round in 2022 out of a junior college (Crowder College), where he started the spring walking a batter an inning but brought that down as the season progressed. While at school, he was already touching 100 mph with a plus slider and great extension out front.
The delivery was still quite rough, and even with the benefit of some of the best stuff in the minors, he still walked almost 15 percent of batters during his time in Double A in 2023 and 2024. He was so inefficient that he’d hit his pitch limits before getting through five innings in the majority of his outings.
His control took another step forward in Triple A to start the 2025 season, and now, improbably, he’s walking just 6.6 percent of batters in the big leagues while throwing harder than any starter in history and doing it with a cleaner, much more repeatable delivery.
Advertisement
There are some small mechanical changes at play in Misiorowski’s ascent, but nothing strikes me as bigger than the fact that he has gotten so much stronger since he was drafted, particularly in his lower half. He’s striding and landing more consistently, and he’s not falling off nearly as hard to the first-base side. When he was in junior college, he’d be lucky to see the plate when he released the ball, with his head snapping hard down to his left at release.
Now he’s throwing harder while looking like he’s expending less effort, which seems hard to believe given that he’s been up to 105 mph and is setting all kinds of records in the pitch-tracking era for velocity. His “Maddux” against the Phillies in May, where he struck out 15, gave up one hit and no other baserunners, and still hit 103.7 mph in the ninth inning, is one of the best pitching performances I’ve ever watched. The Phillies looked like they were swinging toothpicks.
Misiorowski’s development wasn’t accident, but rather the culmination of efforts the Brewers undertook from the moment he joined their organization. After the draft, the Brewers worked right away to get more stability into Misiorowski’s delivery, and to improve his direction so he could be more online to the plate, especially since stuff like his will play in the zone. They also made small changes to simplify the delivery so it would be easier for him to repeat, which might be part of why his stuff has trended upwards if that helped make the delivery more efficient.
He worked with a huge group of Brewers coaches throughout the minors and in the big leagues, including pitching coordinator Nick Childs, assistant pitching coordinator Bryan Leslie and current Giants pitching coach Justin Meccage, who was the pitching coach for Triple-A Nashville last year when Misiorowski started the season there. (Meccage’s nephew, Bryce, is a pitcher in the Brewers’ system.) I thought any team would try to smooth out Miz’s delivery, but that either it would cost him velocity — that the power was the result of the violence, not held back by it, because who thinks a guy throwing 100 could actually be throwing harder if he had better mechanics? — or that it wouldn’t improve his control enough to keep him a starter. Obviously, that didn’t end up being the case. His delivery and command improved and he maintained his elite velocity.
In this annual series, I often try to highlight how I might evaluate a similar prospect differently in the future. In Misiorowski’s case, I don’t know if there’s a lesson to be learned other than it is possible, with n of 1, that a human being can throw this hard this much and be a successful starter, at least for two years, without getting hurt. That’s one datum against all of the pitchers in history who’ve thrown close to this hard and either haven’t held up — Greene’s second Tommy John surgery is the result of at least his third major arm injury — or have had to move to the bullpen, like the other guys I mentioned above. Even Paul Skenes has seen his velocity taper this year.
Advertisement
The base rate for pitchers with this kind of outsized velocity and higher walk rates when younger is still overwhelmingly in the direction of them not sticking as starters. Misiorowski is a unicorn, or a black swan, who at least has shown that staying healthy and throwing strikes with the hardest fastball in history is possible.
Ben Rice, DH/1B/C, New York Yankees
Rice was barely a prospect at all coming up in the Yankees’ system. He was a 2021 12th-round pick out of Dartmouth, where he hit one homer in 30 games (losing almost two seasons to the pandemic).
Even when he started producing in the minor leagues, with a 20-homer season across three levels in 2023, he was old for the levels he played at and didn’t have a position — he was a catcher with no shot to stay there. His swing was extremely uphill, prioritizing power over everything else, and in his first stint in the majors in 2024, pitchers exploited that swing path, leading to his first struggles in pro ball.
Rice went out that offseason and worked on his swing and his body, gaining enough strength to improve his bat speed and, naturally, his contact quality. It wasn’t his first rodeo — he’d changed his stance and swing while in college — but this change was more dramatic, with a much more open setup and a stride that didn’t close himself off, helping him roll over to the right side less often and, at least in 2025, pull the ball in the air more.
The change also made him less vulnerable on stuff middle-in; in 2024, he whiffed on 25 percent of pitches on the inner third, then cut that to 11.3 percent in 2025 and 11.9 percent so far this year. He’s still not a catcher, but he’s a top-10 bat in the majors this year.
I also didn’t have Rice’s teammate, Cam Schlittler, performing as he has in the majors, not when I saw his career-worst outing in Triple A right before he got called up, and not any time before that. He barely threw a sinker at all when I saw him, and used it just 6.1 percent of the time in the majors last year, but this year he’s used it 19.6 percent of the time. Schlittler has thrown something other than one of his three fastballs just 10.6 percent of the time this year. Only Chad Patrick throws fewer non-fastballs among starters with 100+ innings this year; Misiorowski is fourth on the list at 18.3 percent.
Otto Lopez, SS, Miami Marlins
I knew Lopez could play shortstop — that was pretty consistent across all sources — but never had him as a plus defender there. The Blue Jays, his original organization, didn’t seem to view him that way, and ended up selling his contract to the Giants, who then put him on waivers two months later, at which point the Marlins claimed him. And then Miami started him out as their second baseman, where he was a plus defender right away, then moved him to shortstop in 2025 and gave him that job full-time this year, where he’s at plus-10 Outs Above Average with a few weeks to go in the season.
At the plate, he’s always put the ball in play a lot, which I thought would make him a utility infielder, but I wrote before the 2023 season that “he lacks the power or even the impact to be a regular.” That was proven wrong pretty quickly, as even in 2024 he posted a 92 wRC+, close enough to a league-average bat that he was worth over 2 WAR in both the FanGraphs and Baseball-Reference systems. This year, he’s boosted his contact quality even further, with a career-best 40.5 percent hard-hit rate, producing a 116 wRC+ and over 5 WAR already.
Advertisement
I just missed on this one — I was way off on the defense and too light on the offense, treating him like a Nick Madrigal-type hitter who wouldn’t hit the ball hard enough to make his contact ability matter.
Kyle Leahy, RHP, St. Louis Cardinals
I saw Leahy in the Arizona Fall League in 2022, where he posted a 10.67 ERA in 14 1/3 innings, writing afterward that he was a “possible reliever” who was 93-96 with a “decent curveball” and a slider, not mentioning a changeup (I doubt I even saw one) or sweeper.
He’d been a starter that season in Double A, but wasn’t good by any measure. He walked a batter every other inning (11.1 percent) and gave up 22 homers in 141 innings, ending up with an ERA of 5.23. That, oddly enough, was an improvement over 2025, when he was also in Double A and posted an 8.20 ERA, losing his rotation spot in mid-June.
One of the biggest changes for Leahy from his time in the bullpen is that he started pitching in the strike zone more and, of course, brought his walk rate down. In 2024-25, when he made just one start and 111 relief appearances between Triple A and the majors, he walked 45 batters in 164 2/3 innings (6.7 percent). Another change is that he’s ramped up his use of his changeup, using it about 50 percent more often this year than he did in 2025, which was almost twice what he did in 2023, his first year working primarily in relief. Some of his stuff has clearly backed up this year; the curveball was a plus pitch in 2025, but its spin rate is down, and the pitch is breaking less in both directions, so the slider has become his best pitch.
I’m still skeptical about Leahy in the long term; lefties have smoked him this year for a .312/.379/.473 line, and while it’s great that he’s using his changeup more, it’s not that effective of a pitch. But he belongs on this list because I didn’t think there was any way he could go from “excellent 1-2 inning reliever” to “league-average starter,” nor did I think he’d be a starter back in his prospect days.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees news: Aaron Judge expects to be back soon after leg stiffness
item.dc:creator: Jake Devin

item.content:encoded:
Yahoo Sports: As you likely know by now, Aaron Judge exited yesterday's game early when Heliot Ramos pinch-hit for him in the sixth. The Yankees announced it midgame as "lower leg tightness." It's some relief I suppose that Judge didn't re-aggravate the rib fracture that kept him out for over three months, and Judge himself downplayed the seriousness of the ailment after the game.
"We're still trying to ramp up so there's still going to be little things like this that come up," Judge said after the Yankees 13-inning loss to the Twins. "I just thought it would be best instead of pushing through it like I normally do." Judge seemed to view his exit from the game as precautionary, and likened it to the type of thing that would happen in spring training when small, nagging things pop up as players get back into playing shape.
MLB.com | Patrick Donnelly: Clarke Schmidt came off the 60-day injured list yesterday, something we saw coming; he allowed two hits but got two strikeouts while facing four batters in his first MLB action since July 3, 2025. What we didn't see coming was who was pushed off the roster to make room for Schmidt: fan favorite Oswaldo Cabrera. The utilityman Cabrera had spent most of the year at Triple-A, hitting .288 with 19 homers and a .790 OPS, but hasn't spent much time with the big club ever since suffering a brutal ankle injury in a play at home plate last May. Cabrera seems likely to be claimed on waivers, meaning his time in the Bronx is likely to come to an end after being a member of the organization since signing at age-16 in July 2015.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty: ($) Spencer Jones has been a bit of a revelation for the Yankees this year, producing at a high level across the outfield throughout the summer. He's benefited from shadowing another big lefty swinger in the outfield: Cody Bellinger. Bellinger is only 31, but has a very long and decorated track record for a player his age, something Jones has tried to tap into during his time with the Yankees. "As a young guy, I can't help but watch every time he's up there," Jones said of Bellinger. "When we are in the dugout," Jones said, "he's one of those people I can go up to and ask, like, 'Yo, what did you see?' He'll tell me bluntly what he saw, how he saw it, and essentially what he's going to do next time."
New York Daily News | Gary Phillips: Ryan Weathers cleared a key hurdle in his rehab earlier this week, tossing 15 pitches in a bullpen session and sitting 87-90 mph on his fastball. The hope, if things go right, is for the lefty to get into game action before the regular season ends. It's a tight timeline, but with Weathers set to throw another bullpen on Friday before perhaps facing live hitters early next week, it's doable. The Yankees could certainly use his arm in the bullpen as they try to sort out what their playoff relief corps will look like.
FanGraphs | Davy Andrews: This here isn't news, but it is fun. Andrews discusses the Amazon TV show Reacher, in which the titular character tries to maintain a low profile by checking into hotels under aliases, which are always Yankees second basemen. The problem, of course, is that Reacher's cover is often blown, because Yankee second basemen are frequently famous people with recognizable names (don't choose "Starlin Castro" as your alias if you're trying not to attract attention!). So, Andrews endeavors to help Reacher by finding players who played second base for the Yankees who would help Reacher stay undercover. Good aliases include second basemen from New York's Higlander days, like Joe Ward, and Otis Johnson. The worst possible aliases Andrews found? Robinson Canó and Mickey Mantle.

item.title: [nytimes.com] Yankees mailbag: Aaron Judge’s injury, Jasson Domínguez’s future and the playoff rotation
item.dc:creator: Chris Kirschner
item.description: The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode. Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest. Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
